title: Scarcity
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-01 - Scarcity

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain scarcity and identify tradeoffs created by limited resources

Scarcity means people, businesses, and governments have limited resources but unlimited wants. Because resources such as time, money, labor, and raw materials are limited, choices must be made. Every choice involves a tradeoff, and those tradeoffs force individuals and societies to decide how to use scarce resources. Scarcity is the basic problem that economics studies.
Resources are limited, but wants are greater than what can be produced.
A choice must be made between competing uses.
Getting more of one thing means giving up something else.
The question focuses on limits, tradeoffs, or unmet wants.
Scarcity does not mean there is almost none of a good. It means the good is limited relative to wants. Even time and money are scarce because they have alternative uses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING BETWEEN SCARCE USES

A student has two hours before an exam and must choose between studying economics or finishing a history paper. The student cannot fully do both. This is scarcity because time is limited, so choosing one use means giving up the other.
A city has enough money to build either a new park or repair several roads, but not both this year. Why is this an example of scarcity?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Incentives
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-02 - Incentives

blocks.text: Outcome: Predict behavioral responses and unintended consequences created by incentives.

Incentives change the expected benefits or costs of a choice, so they can alter behavior at the margin. The fee alters the next trip's marginal cost, which can change the decision. With limited time, the higher wage makes study more costly in forgone earnings. People respond to incentives, but they may respond in ways that improve the metric while hurting the real goal. The toll raises the cost of using the road, which gives drivers an incentive to change behavior.
A speed bonus makes workers finish faster, but quality falls.
A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road.
A toll is added to a crowded bridge, and some drivers switch routes.
A school rewards high test pass rates.
An incentive changes the payoff to a choice; it need not be monetary or guarantee a result.

A common mistake is to define incentives as cash payments or guaranteed behavior. An incentive changes the expected payoff to a choice; it may be monetary or nonmonetary, and people can respond differently.

A city charges a $4 congestion fee for downtown trips during rush hour. A driver whose next trip provides only $3 of benefit will now avoid that trip because its marginal cost has risen by $4. A commuter whose trip is worth $10 will still travel. The fee changes behavior at the margin without guaranteeing that every driver responds in the same way.
A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Opportunity Cost
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-03 - Opportunity Cost

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify and calculate the value of the next-best alternative.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made. Scarcity makes opportunity cost unavoidable because using time, money, or resources for one purpose prevents their use elsewhere. The cost is the single best forgone option, valued from the decision maker's perspective, and it can be monetary or nonmonetary.
Look for a choice between two or more alternatives under a time, money, or resource constraint.
Identify the next-best alternative that the decision maker gives up.
Value the forgone alternative from the decision maker's perspective.
Do not add every rejected option; opportunity cost is the single best alternative forgone.
A common mistake is to add the value of every forgone option. Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best alternative, not the sum of all alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE NEXT-BEST OPTION

A student can spend Saturday working for $80, studying for an exam worth an estimated $60 benefit, or attending a concert valued at $40. If the student studies, the best forgone alternative is the $80 work shift. The opportunity cost of studying is therefore $80, not $120 and not the concert's $40 value.
Why can spending an hour in a free park have an opportunity cost?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Marginal Analysis
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-04 - Marginal Analysis

blocks.text: Outcome: Use marginal benefits and costs while avoiding sunk-cost reasoning.

Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit of the next unit or small change with its additional cost. A decision should expand while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost and stop before the next unit costs more than it adds. Sunk costs do not affect this forward-looking comparison, while costs or benefits imposed on others matter in social marginal analysis.
Look for a decision about one more unit, one more hour, or a small change in an activity.
Compare the additional benefit of that change with its additional cost.
Continue while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost; stop before the next unit costs more than it adds.
Ignore totals or averages when the question asks whether the next unit is worthwhile.
A common mistake is to decide from total benefit or total cost. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and additional cost of the next unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPARING MARGINAL BENEFIT AND COST

A warehouse earns $15 from handling one additional box, and the marginal cost of that box is $13. Marginal net benefit is $15 - $13 = $2, so handling the box increases profit. If the next box cost $17 instead, its marginal net benefit would be -$2 and the warehouse should stop before that box.
Total cost is $100 for 10 units, and producing an eleventh unit adds $15. Which number is average cost, and which is marginal cost?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-05 - Microeconomics vs. Macroeconomics

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish microeconomic and macroeconomic questions.

Microeconomics studies choices by individual households, firms, workers, and markets, while macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation, and unemployment. One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis. Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets. Macroeconomics examines economy-wide aggregates such as output, inflation, and unemployment. A single firm's hiring decision is microeconomics.
A report tracks national inflation, unemployment, and total output.
A firm decides how much labor to hire at one restaurant.
Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.
A bakery studies how customers respond to a muffin price increase.
Microeconomics studies choices by households, firms, and specific markets.
A common mistake is to label any large organization as macroeconomic. The classification depends on the unit of analysis: one decision-maker is micro; economy-wide aggregates are macro.

A restaurant deciding whether to hire one more server is a microeconomic question because it concerns one firm's choice. The national unemployment rate is a macroeconomic outcome because it aggregates labor-market conditions across the economy. The subject's size is not decisive; the unit of analysis is.
Name three economy-wide outcomes studied in macroeconomics.
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Positive vs. Normative Analysis
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-06 - Positive vs. Normative Analysis

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.

Positive analysis makes claims that evidence can test, while normative analysis applies value judgments about what should be done. Identify what observation could support or contradict a testable claim. A positive claim can be false. A normative claim ranks goals or outcomes using values; evidence can inform that judgment but cannot settle the values alone.
A transit study predicts that a lower fare will increase ridership.
Ridership data can test the prediction even if it turns out to be wrong.
A council member says parks should receive more funding because access is fair.
A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer.
Do not treat positive as good, true, or politically neutral. A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

The statement 'A lower bus fare will increase ridership' is positive because ridership data can support or contradict it. The statement 'The city should lower bus fares because access is fair' is normative because it applies a value judgment. Evidence can inform both statements, but only the first is directly testable as written.
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Models and Assumptions
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-07 - Models and Assumptions

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate the purpose, assumptions, simplifications, and limits of economic models.

Economic models simplify reality to isolate the relationships that matter for a particular question. The two-good abstraction exposes scarcity and opportunity cost without describing every output. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context. Extra complexity is useful only when its benefits exceed lost clarity or robustness. Apply a model where its important assumptions remain reasonable.
Adding dozens of variables improves historical fit but makes the mechanism impossible to interpret.
A central bank changes its policy rule, and a forecasting relationship estimated under the old rule breaks down.
A local haircut model omits exchange rates and global shipping.
An economist builds a simple two-market circular-flow model and leaves out banks, government, and foreign trade.
An economist studies how price affects purchases while holding income constant.
Do not use the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence. Evaluate a model by its purpose, assumptions, performance, and relevant context.

A PPF model includes only two goods, even though real economies produce thousands. That simplification isolates scarcity and opportunity cost: moving toward more of one good requires less of the other. The model is useful for that purpose, but it would be inadequate for predicting the output of a specific industry without additional detail.
What role does an assumption play in a model?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-08 - Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret PPF points, slopes, shifts, efficiency, growth, and opportunity cost.

A production possibilities frontier shows the combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good. Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good. A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.
A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology.
A new technology improves only medical production.
An economy first removes unemployment, then gains new machinery.
Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.

Do not confuse a PPF with a market curve. A PPF shows possible production combinations given current resources and technology. Using idle resources changes the production point; resources or technology shift the frontier.

On the PPF, moving from point C (15 units of X and 35 of Y) to point D (21 of X and 20 of Y) gains 6 units of X but gives up 15 units of Y. The total opportunity cost is 15 units of Y, or 15/6 = 2.5 units of Y per additional unit of X.
Does moving along a PPF represent economic growth?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-09 - Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade.
Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost, even when another producer has an absolute advantage in both goods. Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost. Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain. Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange. Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.
Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.
One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs.
One producer is more productive in both goods.
Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output.

A common mistake is to choose the producer with the greatest absolute output. Comparative advantage depends on lower opportunity cost, and a mutually beneficial terms-of-trade ratio lies between the two opportunity costs.

Ari can produce either 12 lamps or 24 rugs, so one lamp costs Ari 24/12 = 2 rugs. Bea can produce either 10 lamps or 60 rugs, so one lamp costs Bea 60/10 = 6 rugs. Ari has comparative advantage in lamps because 2 rugs is the lower opportunity cost; Bea has comparative advantage in rugs because one rug costs Bea 10/60 = 1/6 lamp, below Ari's 12/24 = 1/2 lamp. Specialization according to those lower opportunity costs can increase combined output.
If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Economists and Policy
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-10 - Economists and Policy

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze the economist's role in policy advice.

Economists use evidence and models to estimate policy effects, identify tradeoffs, and explain uncertainty. Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences. Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal. Economists can estimate consequences; recommendations also require value judgments. Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
An economist estimates a policy’s effects, then recommends adoption.
Economists analyze incentives, evidence, and tradeoffs; elected officials make policy choices.
Policy evaluation requires explicit objectives and evidence about consequences.
A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period.
Good advice makes assumptions, tradeoffs, and uncertainty visible.
A common mistake is to give economists authority to choose society's values. Economists can estimate consequences and tradeoffs; the policy choice also requires normative judgments.

An economist estimates that a proposed transit subsidy will increase ridership by 8%, but the estimate comes from a city with denser development. Professional advice reports the predicted benefit, explains the uncertain transfer to the local setting, and identifies fiscal costs. Whether those consequences justify the policy also depends on public values and priorities.
Is a policy forecast a guarantee?

title: Competitive Markets
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-11 - Competitive Markets

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify the conditions that create price-taking behavior and limited market power

A competitive market contains many independent buyers and sellers, usually trading products that buyers view as close substitutes. No single participant controls enough of the market to set the market price. A small firm is therefore a price taker: it chooses how much to sell at the price created by market supply and demand. Competition becomes stronger when firms can enter or exit, buyers can compare offers, and switching among sellers is easy.
Many independent firms sell the same product or close substitutes.
One seller supplies only a small share of total market output.
A firm accepts a price determined by overall market supply and demand.
Buyers can compare prices and switch sellers without much difficulty.
Entry by new firms or exit by existing firms changes competitive pressure.

A market is not strictly competitive just because it has several sellers. Product differentiation, search costs, network effects, or barriers to entry can still give firms pricing power. The key question is whether one seller can raise its price persistently without losing many customers to available alternatives.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING A PRICE TAKER

A wheat farmer is one of thousands selling a standardized crop. The posted market price is $6 per bushel. If this farmer asks $7 while other farmers still charge $6, buyers can purchase identical wheat elsewhere. The farmer is too small to move the market price, so raising the price would sharply reduce sales. The evidence - many sellers, a standardized product, and easy switching - identifies price-taking behavior.
An online marketplace makes prices easy to compare, but a merger leaves one company controlling most available inventory. Which fact strengthens competition, which fact weakens it, and why?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Demand & the Law of Demand
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-12 - Demand & the Law of Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain demand, quantity demanded, and movements along a demand curve.

Demand describes the quantities buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices, holding other demand conditions constant. Quantity demanded is the amount buyers choose at one particular price. The law of demand states that a lower own price increases quantity demanded and a higher own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same demand curve; it does not shift the curve.
The good's own price changes while income, tastes, expectations, related-good prices, and the number of buyers remain constant.
The question asks for quantity demanded at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same downward-sloping demand curve.
A lower price is paired with a larger quantity demanded.

A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in demand. If the good's own price changes and buyers move from one point to another on the same demand curve, quantity demanded changes. Demand itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

On the gourmet-donut graph, point A shows a price of $10 and quantity demanded of 100 thousand. Point B shows a lower price of $5 and quantity demanded of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same demand curve and only the good's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity demanded of 125 thousand, not an increase in demand.
The price of a concert ticket falls and buyers move to another point on the same demand curve. What changes: demand or quantity demanded?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Determinants of Demand
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-13 - Determinants of Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.

Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.

At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Supply & the Law of Supply
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-14 - Supply & the Law of Supply

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain supply, quantity supplied, and movements along a supply curve.

Supply describes the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices, holding other supply conditions constant. Quantity supplied is the amount sellers offer at one particular price. The law of supply states that a higher own price generally increases quantity supplied and a lower own price decreases it, all else equal. An own-price change causes movement between points on the same supply curve; it does not shift the curve.
The good's own price changes while production conditions remain constant.
The question asks for quantity supplied at a particular price.
Two points lie on the same upward-sloping supply curve.
A higher price is paired with a larger quantity supplied.

A common mistake is to call every change in quantity a shift in supply. If the good's own price changes and sellers move from one point to another on the same supply curve, quantity supplied changes. Supply itself shifts only when a nonprice determinant changes.

On the coffee supply graph, point A shows a price of $6 and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Point B shows a higher price of $11 and quantity supplied of 225 thousand. Because both points lie on the same supply curve and only coffee's own price changes, the move from A to B is an increase in quantity supplied of 125 thousand, not an increase in supply.
The market price of handmade tables rises and sellers move to another point on the same supply curve. What changes?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Determinants of Supply
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-15 - Determinants of Supply

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift supply left or right.

Supply shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Supply increases and shifts right when sellers can provide more at every price; supply decreases and shifts left when they provide less at every price. Important determinants include input and resource costs, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, the number of sellers, and natural or regulatory production conditions. A change that lowers marginal production cost generally increases supply, while a change that raises marginal cost generally decreases it.
Input prices, technology, productivity, taxes, or subsidies change.
Producers' expectations or the number of sellers changes.
Quantity supplied changes at the same price.
The entire supply curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a supply shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A change in production cost, technology, expectations, or the number of sellers changes how much firms offer at every price and shifts the curve.

At a hamburger price of $9, the original curve S0 shows quantity supplied of 200 thousand, while S1 shows 100 thousand. The product's price is unchanged, so the 100-thousand decrease is not a movement along S0. It is a leftward shift from S0 to S1, consistent with a determinant such as higher input costs reducing supply.
A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels. Which direction does supply shift, and why?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Market Equilibrium
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-16 - Market Equilibrium

blocks.text: Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

On the graph, the new demand and supply curves intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. The intersection is the only point at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so it is the new market equilibrium. A price above $5 would create a surplus, while a price below $5 would create a shortage.
Holding supply constant, which equilibrium outcome follows from an increase in demand?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Shortages and Surpluses
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-17 - Shortages and Surpluses

blocks.text: Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.

A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied; a surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. A surplus occurs when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward. A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
At the current price, buyers want 180 units and sellers offer 120 units.
A price above equilibrium creates a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded.
A common mistake is to reverse shortage and price pressure. Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, so there is a shortage. Shortages push price upward.

At a price of $2 per gallon, the graph shows quantity demanded of 200 thousand gallons and quantity supplied of 100 thousand. Because buyers want 100 thousand more gallons than sellers offer, the market has a shortage of 200 - 100 = 100 thousand gallons. Upward pressure on price follows.
At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Simultaneous Shifts
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-18 - Simultaneous Shifts

blocks.text: Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.

When demand and supply shift at the same time, each shift contributes separately to the new equilibrium. Analyze how each change affects price and quantity, then combine the directional effects. If both shifts push one variable in the same direction, that result is determinate; if they push in opposite directions, the result depends on the relative size of the shifts.
Both a demand determinant and a supply determinant change.
A bicycle endorsement raises demand while higher input costs reduce supply.
Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and quantity effects.
Opposing effects on one variable leave its direction ambiguous unless relative shift sizes are known.

Do not assume an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts. A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMBINING DEMAND AND SUPPLY SHIFTS

The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 and quantity of 150 thousand. After demand shifts right to D1 and supply shifts left to S1, the new intersection is $5 and the same quantity of 150 thousand. Both shifts raise price; their opposing quantity effects happen to offset in this graph, though quantity would otherwise be ambiguous.
Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Price Ceilings
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-19 - Price Ceilings

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding ceilings and analyze shortages and rationing.

A price ceiling sets a legal maximum price and is binding only when it lies below the market equilibrium price. A binding ceiling keeps price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops. A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
Compare the legal maximum price with the market equilibrium price.
A ceiling below equilibrium is binding and creates excess demand.
At the ceiling price, read quantity demanded and quantity supplied; their difference is the shortage.
A ceiling at or above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
A common mistake is to assume that every price ceiling is binding. A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.

The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding ceiling of $20 holds price below equilibrium; buyers demand 250 units while sellers supply 150. The resulting shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some willing buyers cannot purchase at the controlled price.
At a binding price ceiling, Qd = 90 and Qs = 60. What is the shortage?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Price Floors
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-20 - Price Floors

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding floors and analyze surpluses and unintended effects.

A price floor sets a legal minimum price and is binding only when it lies above the market equilibrium price. A binding floor keeps price from falling to equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus develops. A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
Compare the legal minimum price with the market equilibrium price.
A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates excess supply.
At the floor price, read quantity supplied and quantity demanded; their difference is the surplus.
A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
A common mistake is to assume that every price floor is binding. Equilibrium is $30. A floor at $20 is below equilibrium, so it does not prevent the market from reaching $30.

The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding floor of $40 holds price above equilibrium; sellers offer 250 units while buyers demand 150. The resulting surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some output remains unsold at the controlled price.
At a binding price floor, Qs = 110 and Qd = 80. What is the surplus?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Tax Incidence without Elasticity
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-21 - Tax Incidence without Elasticity

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish legal tax assignment from economic burden.

A tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden. Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.
Look for a per-unit tax that separates the price buyers pay from the price sellers receive.
Find the new quantity where the vertical gap between demand and supply equals the tax.
The buyer burden is the rise in the buyer price; the seller burden is the fall in the seller price.
Do not infer burden from who sends the tax payment to the government.
A common mistake is to assume that legal tax assignment determines the full economic burden. Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING A TAX WEDGE

Before the tax, buyers and sellers trade at $10.50. After the tax is imposed on buyers, the graph shows buyers paying $13.50 while sellers receive $7.50. Each side is $3 away from the original price, so each bears half of the $6 tax even though buyers are legally responsible for remitting it.
At the post-tax quantity of 60 thousand movies, what price do sellers receive according to the supply curve?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Tax Incidence with Elasticity
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-22 - Tax Incidence with Elasticity

blocks.text: Outcome: Use elasticity to determine and calculate the distribution of tax burdens.

Tax incidence depends on relative elasticity: the less responsive side of the market bears more of the tax burden. That side changes quantity less when the tax alters the price it pays or receives, so more of the tax wedge appears on its side of the market. Legal responsibility for remitting the tax does not determine its economic burden.
The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden; identify that side from the market conditions.
A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in quantity but a large increase in buyer price.
In one market, demand is much more elastic than supply.

A common mistake is to assume that the more elastic side bears more of a tax. The less elastic side bears more. In this particular worked graph, the price changes show an equal split; do not assume buyers always bear more.

The untaxed equilibrium price is $15. With the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and 80 units are sold. Buyers bear $18 - $15 = $3 per unit, so their total burden is $3 x 80 = $240. Sellers bear the remaining $3 per unit.
When demand is less elastic than supply, which side is less able to avoid the tax?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: International Trade: World Prices
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-23 - International Trade: World Prices

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret International Trade: World Prices.

A world price lets a small country trade at a price determined outside its domestic market. When the world price is below the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply and the country imports the difference. When the world price is above the no-trade price, domestic firms supply more than buyers demand and the country exports the difference. Trade changes domestic production, consumption, and the distribution of surplus.
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
A world price below the no-trade price makes the country an importer.
A world price above the no-trade price makes the country an exporter.
At the world price, imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus quantity supplied; exports use the reverse difference.
Do not use high demand instead of world price comparison. A lower world price creates excess domestic demand that is filled by imports.

The domestic no-trade equilibrium price is $7. When the country opens to free trade at a world price of $5, domestic buyers demand more than domestic firms supply, and imports fill the difference. Because the world price is below the no-trade price, the country is an importer of this good.
A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: International Trade: Tariffs
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-24 - International Trade: Tariffs

blocks.text: A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price. Domestic firms respond by producing more, consumers buy less, and imports fall. Consumers lose surplus, domestic producers gain surplus, and the government collects tariff revenue. The tariff also prevents mutually beneficial trades, creating deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
Begin with an importing country whose world price is below the domestic no-trade price.
Add the tariff per unit to the world price to find the tariff-inclusive domestic price.
At that higher price, read domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied; imports equal their difference.
Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the number of units imported.
Look for lower consumer surplus, higher producer surplus, government revenue, and deadweight loss from overproduction and underconsumption.
Do not treat tariff revenue as full welfare loss. Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

At the $4 world price, domestic quantity demanded is 250 thousand and domestic quantity supplied is 50 thousand, so free-trade imports are 200 thousand. A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $6; quantity demanded falls to 200 thousand and quantity supplied rises to 100 thousand. Imports fall to 100 thousand, and government tariff revenue is $2 x 100 thousand = $200 thousand.
Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: International Trade: Quotas
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-25 - International Trade: Quotas

blocks.text: An import quota directly limits the quantity of a good that may enter the country. A binding quota reduces imports below their free-trade level, raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption. The price gap between the domestic quota price and the world price creates quota rent. Who receives that rent affects the country's national-surplus result, while the production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
Begin with the free-trade outcome at the world price.
A binding import quota limits imports below their free-trade quantity.
The restriction raises domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption.
The gap between the quota price and world price creates quota rent on each permitted import.
Look for deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.

Do not assume quota rent automatically becomes government revenue. It accrues to whoever holds the import rights; auctioning those rights can transfer the rent to government. The recipient matters for national welfare, while production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: QUOTA PRICE AND IMPORTS

Before trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at a price of $7. With free trade, buyers can purchase at the $3 world price, which creates imports. The quota limits imports, so the domestic price rises to $6. The difference between the $6 quota price and the $3 world price is $3 per imported unit; that $3 gap is quota rent.
A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: International Trade: Policy and Distribution
documentTitle: General Economics GEN-ECON-26 - International Trade: Policy and Distribution

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate International Trade: Policy and Distribution.

Trade protection redistributes income and usually reduces total surplus, so a policy claim must be evaluated against its costs and alternatives. Security, infant-industry, employment, and bargaining arguments may identify legitimate goals, but each claim requires evidence that the policy can achieve the goal and that a less costly policy is unavailable. Sound analysis separates measurable economic effects from the value judgments used to choose among them.
Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison.
Compare the free-trade and quota outcomes.
An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution.
Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.

Do not ignore efficiency or distribution evidence. Security can be legitimate, but the claim still requires evidence and comparison. An infant-industry argument requires a temporary, evidence-based learning mechanism and net benefits.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING A TRADE-POLICY CLAIM

Suppose protection preserves 1,000 domestic jobs but costs consumers $30 million each year. The positive analysis reports both effects and asks whether less costly policies could assist affected workers. The normative decision then weighs security, distribution, and adjustment goals against the efficiency cost. Saying only that protection 'saves jobs' leaves the consumer cost and alternatives unexamined.
What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: GDP Measurement
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-01 - GDP Measurement

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply GDP inclusion rules and explain why measured expenditure equals measured income

Gross domestic product is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period. Current production matters: used goods, stocks, bonds, and transfer payments do not represent newly produced output. Final goods are counted instead of adding intermediate goods separately, because the intermediate value is already included in the final product. The location of production, not the owner's nationality, determines whether output is domestic. Measured expenditure equals measured income because a buyer's spending becomes income to the sellers and workers who produced the output.
The good or service was produced during the period being measured.
Production occurred inside the country's borders, regardless of ownership.
A final product is distinguished from an input used to make another product.
A resale, financial trade, or transfer changes ownership but adds no current output.
One transaction is viewed as both buyer expenditure and seller income.

Spending money does not automatically create GDP. A used-car sale, stock purchase, or cash transfer may be a transaction without current production. Also, adding the value of an intermediate input and the final good double counts the input. Imports are excluded because they were produced abroad, even when domestic residents buy them.

A mill sells flour to a bakery for $50, and the bakery sells the finished bread to households for $120. Final-goods accounting counts $120, not $170, because the flour's value is already embodied in the bread. The households' $120 of expenditure becomes revenue and income for the producers involved. Counting the same production from the expenditure side or the income side therefore gives the same GDP amount.
A U.S.-owned factory makes a car in Mexico, while a Japanese-owned factory makes a car in Ohio. Which car belongs in U.S. GDP, and what rule determines the answer?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: GDP Components
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-02 - GDP Components

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.

The expenditure approach divides GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Consumption covers household purchases of final goods and services; investment includes business capital, residential construction, and inventory changes; government purchases pay for current goods and services. Net exports add exports and subtract imports so GDP counts only domestic production, while transfer payments themselves are excluded. A recipient's later purchase is counted separately if it pays for current domestic output.
Classify final spending as consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports.
Count newly produced capital goods and inventory changes as investment.
Exclude transfer payments because they are not payments for current production.
Subtract imports within net exports so foreign production is not counted in domestic GDP.

A common mistake is to count transfer payments as government purchases. Transfers redistribute income and are never themselves part of GDP. A later purchase is classified by what is bought; imports are subtracted in NX.

A business buys a newly produced domestic machine for $2 million; this is investment. Government pays contractors $80 million to repair roads; this is government purchases. An $80 million benefit payment is a transfer and is not counted when sent, though any later household purchase of final goods enters consumption. The expenditure identity classifies the counted spending as C + I + G + NX.
Does a government benefit payment enter G when it is sent?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Real versus Nominal GDP
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-03 - Real versus Nominal GDP

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.

Nominal GDP values current production at current prices, while real GDP values it at base-year prices. Multiply current quantities by the designated base-year prices and add across final goods. GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare. Compare nominal and real GDP to separate price changes from changes in production. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
Nominal GDP uses current-year prices and current-year quantities.
Real GDP uses base-year prices with current-year quantities.
A change in nominal GDP can reflect prices, quantities, or both; a change in real GDP reflects quantities.
Use the GDP deflator to compare nominal GDP with real GDP for the same year.
Do not use the new level rather than the initial real-GDP level as the percentage-growth denominator. Real-GDP growth equals the change in real GDP divided by the initial real GDP.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SEPARATING PRICE AND OUTPUT CHANGES

An economy produces 100 units in the base year at $5 each and 110 units this year at $6 each. Nominal GDP this year is 110 x $6 = $660. Real GDP at base-year prices is 110 x $5 = $550. The GDP deflator is ($660 / $550) x 100 = 120, separating the price increase from the output increase.
Is real GDP calculated by simply subtracting the inflation rate from nominal GDP?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Limits of GDP
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-04 - Limits of GDP

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate GDP as a measure of well-being.

GDP measures market production, not every dimension of well-being. GDP can rise from replacement activity even if people are worse off. GDP is useful, but it is not a complete measure of well-being. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently. GDP is useful because income matters, but it leaves out things like leisure, environmental quality, and some nonmarket activity.
A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals.
Unpaid elder care becomes an otherwise similar paid service.
A country has higher GDP, but also more pollution and longer work hours.
A free digital service replaces a paid service while users receive greater benefit.
A free technology replaces paid translation services, measured GDP falls, and users translate more text with less effort.

A common mistake is to equate a change in market spending with the same change in total useful services. Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding adds $2 billion to measured construction. Holding other domestic production constant, rebuilding adds $2 billion to GDP. It does not subtract the homes that were destroyed or the loss of security and leisure, so the GDP increase does not prove that well-being improved.
GDP misses which part of well-being?

title: CPI and Inflation Measurement
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-05 - CPI and Inflation Measurement

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate CPI and inflation using a market basket.

The consumer price index compares the current cost of a fixed consumer basket with its base-year cost. The index equals the current basket cost divided by the base-year basket cost, multiplied by one hundred. Inflation is the percentage change in the index between periods. Holding basket quantities fixed isolates price change from changes in what consumers buy.
Identify the fixed basket, its base-year cost, and its current-year cost.
Compute the price index by comparing the current basket cost with the base-year basket cost.
Measure inflation as the percentage change in the index from one period to the next.
Keep basket quantities fixed when calculating the CPI for different years.
Do not use the wrong basket cost or forget to multiply by 100. Divide the current cost of the fixed basket by its base-year cost; the index can rise or fall as prices change.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING CPI AND INFLATION

The CPI rises from 125 to 150. The inflation rate is (150 - 125)/125 x 100 = 20%. In a separate basket, base-year cost is 4($10) + 2($20) = $80 and current cost is 4($12) + 2($25) = $98, so CPI is ($98/$80) x 100 = 122.5.
A basket costs $400 in the base year and $500 today. What is today's CPI?

title: CPI Bias
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-06 - CPI Bias

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze substitution, quality, and new-goods bias.

The CPI can overstate changes in the cost of living when a fixed basket misses substitution, quality improvements, or new goods. Substitution bias arises when consumers shift toward relatively cheaper alternatives but the fixed basket does not fully reflect that response. CPI remains useful, while substitution, new-good, and quality challenges can make measured inflation differ from true cost-of-living growth. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living. If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.
If consumers substitute, their actual cost of living may rise less than the fixed basket suggests.
A new product gives consumers a useful option that did not previously exist.
A product becomes more expensive but also much higher quality.
A laptop price rises while speed and battery life improve.
Do not treat all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves. If goods improve in quality, price increases may overstate the rise in the cost of living.

A fixed basket contains beef even after beef prices rise sharply. Consumers substitute toward chicken, but the CPI continues pricing the original beef quantity. Because the fixed basket misses that cost-saving response, measured inflation can exceed the increase in the cost of maintaining consumers' actual purchasing pattern.
A refrigerator sells for the same price but uses much less electricity and lasts longer. Which CPI issue matters?

title: CPI versus GDP Deflator
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-07 - CPI versus GDP Deflator

blocks.text: Outcome: Compare the construction and uses of CPI and the GDP deflator.

The CPI tracks prices paid for a consumer basket, while the GDP deflator tracks prices of currently produced domestic final output. Imported consumer goods affect CPI but not the GDP deflator directly. Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP. Identify the buyer and production location, then match the price change to the index whose scope includes it. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
Use CPI for consumer purchasing-power questions and the GDP deflator for the price level of current domestic GDP.
A domestic firm buys newly produced business software whose price rises.
Imported prescription-drug prices rise while prices of domestic hospital services are unchanged.
A city buys domestic transit vehicles while households buy imported fuel.
Domestic food-export prices rise and imported-clothing prices fall.

Do not treat CPI and the GDP deflator as interchangeable measures of the same set of prices. CPI follows a consumer-basket framework; the GDP deflator follows prices of current domestically produced final output.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CHOOSING THE RIGHT PRICE INDEX

The price of imported coffee rises while prices of domestically produced goods are unchanged. Coffee is in the consumer basket, so the increase can raise CPI. Because the coffee was produced abroad, it is not part of domestic GDP and does not directly raise the GDP deflator.
Which price index uses a fixed basket of consumer goods?

title: Indexing and Real Values
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-08 - Indexing and Real Values

blocks.text: Outcome: Convert nominal values across time and apply indexation.

A price index converts nominal amounts across time and can be used to index wages, benefits, rents, or tax thresholds. Converting an earlier nominal amount into later dollars requires multiplying by the later index divided by the earlier index. Indexation preserves purchasing power only when the chosen index and adjustment timing closely match the prices relevant to the recipient.
Identify the nominal amount, the starting index, and the ending index.
Scale the nominal amount by the ratio of the ending index to the starting index.
Check whether the contract uses the same index and adjustment timing as the prices relevant to the recipient.
A fully indexed nominal payment preserves purchasing power only to the extent that the index matches actual costs.

Do not assume an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INDEXING A NOMINAL PAYMENT

A salary was $40,000 when CPI was 100. CPI is now 160. 40,000 x 160/100 = 64,000. Therefore, $64,000. Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.
Why might a tax threshold be indexed to a price index?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Real versus Nominal Interest Rates
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-09 - Real versus Nominal Interest Rates

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate and interpret real and nominal interest rates.

The real interest rate approximately equals the nominal interest rate minus inflation. The nominal rate states how many additional dollars a lender receives, while the real rate measures the change in purchasing power. Expected inflation determines the ex ante real rate when a loan is made; actual inflation determines the ex post real return and can redistribute purchasing power between borrowers and lenders.
Unexpected inflation is higher than lenders and borrowers expected on a fixed-rate loan.
Actual inflation is lower than expected on a fixed nominal loan.
Unexpected inflation rises on a fixed-rate loan.
Actual inflation exceeds expected inflation while a loan’s nominal rate is fixed.
Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.

Do not use actual inflation to describe an expected return or expected inflation to describe the realized return. Ex ante real interest uses expected inflation; ex post real interest uses actual inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING THE REAL INTEREST RATE

Nominal interest is 9% and inflation is 5%. Using the usual approximation, real interest is 9% - 5% = 4%. The exact real return is (1.09 / 1.05 - 1) x 100 = 3.81%. Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.
What does a real interest rate describe that a nominal rate does not?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Living Standards and Growth
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-10 - Living Standards and Growth

blocks.text: Outcome: Use real GDP per person and compounding to compare living standards.

Real GDP per person is a common measure of material living standards, and compounding makes sustained growth powerful over time. Dividing real output by population distinguishes growth in total production from growth in average material resources. Productivity growth can raise output per person without requiring proportionally more work, although this measure does not capture every dimension of well-being.
A country raises output mainly by requiring much longer workweeks, while output per hour is unchanged.
Higher productivity lets an economy produce more goods and services from its available labor and resources.
Real GDP per person is commonly used to compare living standards and growth.
Real GDP per person relates inflation-adjusted output to the number of people sharing that output.
Compare growth in real GDP with population growth to distinguish total output from output per person.

A common mistake is to equate more total labor input with higher productivity or complete welfare improvement. Productivity is output per unit of input, and GDP omits important dimensions of well-being.

If real GDP per person grows at 4% per year, the Rule of 70 estimates a doubling time of 70/4 = 17.5 years. This calculation describes material output growth, not complete well-being: longer work hours can raise GDP per person without raising output per hour or preserving leisure.
At 4% annual growth, about how many years does the Rule of 70 predict for real GDP per person to double?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Productivity Measurement
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-11 - Productivity Measurement

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.

Labor productivity measures output per worker or per hour worked. For example, 2,400 units produced in 300 labor hours means 2,400 / 300 = 8 units per hour. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter. A country can consume more when its workers produce more output per worker.
Measure labor productivity as real output per worker or per hour worked.
Compare output using the same amount of labor when evaluating a productivity change.
An increase in total output is not necessarily a productivity increase if labor input also rises.
On a production-function graph, diminishing returns make equal additions of capital add progressively less output.
Do not confuse total output with output per unit of labor. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.

The graph shows output per worker of 28.53 when capital per worker is 20 and 36.37 when capital per worker is 40. The increase in labor productivity is 36.37 - 28.53 = 7.84 units per worker. Productivity measures output relative to labor input, not total output alone.
A business uses more labor hours but produces the same amount of output. What happens to labor productivity?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Sources of Productivity
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-12 - Sources of Productivity

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

Productivity rises with physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technological knowledge. Capital can have high returns where it is scarce. More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens. Productivity compares output with the labor input used to produce it, so changes in both output and labor matter.
A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time.
More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens.
The graph is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises.
A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity.
Do not treat every increase in capital as producing the same output gain. More capital per worker can raise output per worker, but the production function becomes flatter as capital deepens.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CAPITAL DEEPENING AND PRODUCTIVITY

Increasing capital per worker from 20 to 40 raises output per worker from 28.53 to 36.37, a gain of 7.84. The production function becomes flatter as capital deepens, so equal additions to capital generate progressively smaller output gains. That curvature shows diminishing returns to capital.
How does a worker's machine differ from the worker's training as a source of productivity?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Economic Growth Policy
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-13 - Economic Growth Policy

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate policies affecting long-run productivity and growth.

Long-run growth policy raises productive capacity rather than current spending alone. Saving and reliable finance support capital formation; education builds human capital; research and competition can advance technology. Stable property rights and institutions make firms more willing to invest. Because physical capital faces diminishing returns, sustained growth usually depends on several of these channels working together.
The policy changes capital formation, human capital, technology, or institutions.
The question distinguishes productive capacity from a temporary demand increase.
Reliable finance and property rights affect whether saving becomes productive investment.
The proposed change can raise output per worker over time.

Do not treat a one-time demand boost as a substitute for policies that raise productive capacity. Long-run growth policy works through productivity, capital formation, human capital, technology, and institutions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EVALUATING A GROWTH POLICY

Capital deepening from 20 to 40 units per worker raises output per worker from 28.53 to 36.37, a gain of 7.84. Because the curve flattens, capital accumulation alone faces diminishing returns. Sustained growth also requires human capital, technology, and institutions that raise productivity.
Which policy supports long-run productivity growth?

title: Unemployment Measurement
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-14 - Unemployment Measurement

blocks.text: Outcome: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

Labor-force status depends on work, job attachment, availability, and active job search. Employed people include those working for pay or profit, those temporarily absent from a job, and qualifying unpaid family workers. Unemployed people have no job, are available, and actively searched in the past four weeks; people awaiting recall from temporary layoff need not search. Discouraged workers who have stopped searching are outside the labor force.
Work for pay or profit during the reference week counts as employment, even if part-time.
At least 15 hours of unpaid work in a family business also counts as employment.
Labor force = employed + unemployed; unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force x 100.
Participation rate = labor force / civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older x 100.
Wanting a job alone does not make a person unemployed. Check job status, availability, and active search, including the temporary-layoff exception. Discouraged workers are outside the labor force.

Among 100 people in the civilian noninstitutional population age 16 and older, 60 are employed, 5 are unemployed, and 35 are outside the labor force. Labor force = 60 + 5 = 65. Unemployment rate = 5/65 x 100 = 7.7%; participation rate = 65/100 x 100 = 65%.
Which two groups are added to calculate the labor force?

title: Types of Unemployment
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-15 - Types of Unemployment

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.

Frictional unemployment comes from ordinary job search, structural unemployment from lasting mismatches, and cyclical unemployment from recessions. Layoffs caused by recession are cyclical unemployment. Short-term search between jobs is frictional unemployment. Job loss from weak demand during a recession is cyclical unemployment. A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.
A worker loses a job because a recession causes customers to spend less.
A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills.
Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.
Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.
A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills.

Do not confuse the cause of unemployment with official labor-force status. For a jobless worker who is available and actively searching, normal search after leaving a job is frictional unemployment; recession-related job loss is cyclical unemployment.

A worker leaves a job and spends six weeks searching for a better match; that is frictional unemployment. A factory worker whose skills no longer match available technology faces structural unemployment. A restaurant worker laid off because a recession reduces spending experiences cyclical unemployment.
A worker quits and spends two weeks finding a better job match. What type of unemployment is this?

title: Labor-Market Institutions
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-16 - Labor-Market Institutions

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze minimum wages, unions, job search, and efficiency wages.

Labor-market institutions change wages, hiring, search incentives, and the balance between labor supplied and labor demanded. Efficiency wages can improve effort and reduce turnover. A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire. Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.
A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire.
Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.
A firm raises wages above equilibrium and worker effort rises enough to improve productivity, but fewer workers are hired at the higher wage.
Unemployment insurance can reduce the cost of continued job search, which may lengthen unemployment spells.
Union wage bargaining can raise wages above equilibrium and reduce the quantity of labor demanded.

Do not forget that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded. A binding minimum wage can create a surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire.

At a binding minimum wage, 120 workers want jobs and firms hire 90. The labor surplus is 120 - 90 = 30 workers. The wage is held above equilibrium, so the quantity of labor supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.
Why can more generous unemployment insurance lengthen some unemployment spells even while protecting workers?

title: Natural Rate of Unemployment
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-17 - Natural Rate of Unemployment

blocks.text: Outcome: Separate the natural unemployment benchmark from business-cycle unemployment

The natural rate of unemployment is the unemployment that remains when the economy is operating near its normal long-run level. It includes frictional unemployment from ordinary job search and structural unemployment from mismatches between workers and available jobs. It excludes cyclical unemployment caused by recessions or unusually strong expansions. Actual unemployment can move above or below the natural rate over the business cycle. Cyclical unemployment equals actual unemployment minus the natural rate. The natural rate can also change as demographics, labor-market institutions, matching technology, or persistent skill mismatches change.
Frictional and structural unemployment are combined into a long-run benchmark.
A recession pushes actual unemployment above the benchmark.
An unusually tight labor market pushes actual unemployment below the benchmark.
Job matching, worker skills, demographics, or institutions change over time.
The problem asks for the gap between actual and natural unemployment.

The natural rate is neither zero nor permanently fixed. Workers still search for jobs and industries still change in a healthy economy. A temporary recession raises cyclical unemployment, not automatically the natural rate; however, lasting skill loss or labor-force detachment can eventually raise structural unemployment and the natural rate.

Suppose actual unemployment is 7% and the natural rate is 5%. Cyclical unemployment = 7% - 5% = 2 percentage points. The positive gap indicates recession-related unemployment on top of normal frictional and structural unemployment. If demand recovers and the natural rate remains 5%, actual unemployment should move back toward 5%. It need not fall to zero because normal job search and skill mismatch remain.
A job-matching platform shortens job searches, but a major industry shift leaves many workers without the skills employers need. How could each change affect the natural rate?
Return to the game and master this concept.

The natural rate can also change as demographics, labor-market institutions, matching technology, or persistent skill mismatches change.

title: Money Functions and Measures
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-18 - Money Functions and Measures

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify money's functions, forms, and M1/M2 measurement.

Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. As a medium of exchange it facilitates purchases; as a unit of account it provides a common way to quote prices and debts; as a store of value it carries purchasing power into the future. Money-supply measures group liquid assets by how readily they can perform these functions.
A medium of exchange is used to buy and sell goods and services.
A unit of account provides the common measure in which prices and debts are stated.
A store of value transfers purchasing power from the present into the future.
For a money-supply measure, classify an asset by its liquidity and the measure's stated definition.

Do not treat movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2. Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

Currency is $800, checking deposits are $1,200, and savings deposits are $1,500. Under the U.S. definition used since May 2020, savings deposits are included in M1, so M1 = $3,500. With no other M2 components, M2 is also $3,500. Under the older textbook definition excluding savings from M1, M1 would be $2,000.
Are retail money-market mutual funds included in M1, M2, or both?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Central Banking and the Federal Reserve
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-19 - Central Banking and the Federal Reserve

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain central-bank structure, roles, independence, and the FOMC.
Central Banking and the Federal Reserve

The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy, supplies reserve balances, supports payments, and serves as lender of last resort. Changes in reserves and interest rates are monetary policy territory. The Fed acts as the central bank and lender of last resort. The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations. Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks. The Fed includes the Board of Governors and 12 regional Reserve Banks. The FOMC directs monetary policy. Operational independence allows policy decisions without day-to-day political approval, within a mandate set by Congress.
The Federal Reserve conducts monetary policy and supports the banking/payments system; the Treasury manages federal finances and debt operations.
The FOMC sets the monetary-policy stance and directs open-market operations.
A central-bank committee decides to change monetary conditions.
A commercial bank approves a loan and credits the borrower’s checking account.
Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.

Do not treat commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves as the same liability issued by the same institution. Commercial banks create deposit liabilities when they lend; the central bank creates reserve balances/base money used by banks.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CENTRAL BANK OR TREASURY?

The Federal Reserve buys Treasury securities from a bank, adding reserve balances. In the limited-reserves textbook model, this tends to lower short-term rates; in an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main rate-control tool. The purchase is monetary policy, not a change in federal taxes or spending.

title: Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
documentTitle: MACRO-20 - Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital

blocks.text: Classify bank accounts and trace how transactions
Bank Balance Sheets, Reserves, and Capital
A bank balance sheet satisfies assets = liabilities + capital. Reserves, loans, and securities are assets. Deposits and bank borrowing are
liabilities. Bank capital is owners' equity: assets minus liabilities. Reserves provide liquidity and help meet withdrawals; capital absorbs
asset losses. Required reserves and capital requirements therefore constrain different parts of the balance sheet.
A customer's deposit is a bank liability; the cash or reserve balance received is an asset.
A cash withdrawal reduces both reserves and deposits by the same amount.
A loan is a bank asset because the borrower owes the bank repayment.
An asset loss reduces capital when liabilities do not change.

WORKED EXAMPLE: CAPITAL ABSORBS AN ASSET LOSS
A bank holds $120 in reserves, $780 in loans, and $100 in securities: assets
are $1,000. Deposits of $900 and borrowing of $40 make liabilities $940, so
capital is $60. A $25 loan loss cuts assets to $975 while liabilities stay $940.
If a depositor withdraws $20 in cash, which asset and which liability fall?

title: Monetary-Policy Tools
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-21 - Monetary-Policy Tools

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply open-market operations, administered rates, and reserve tools.

The Federal Reserve influences bank reserves, the money supply, and short-term interest rates through several policy tools. Open-market purchases add reserves to the banking system, while open-market sales remove them. Administered rates change the incentives banks face when borrowing or holding reserves. Changes in reserves can affect bank lending and deposit creation, although the actual expansion of money may be smaller than the simple textbook multiplier predicts.
An open-market purchase adds reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to lower short-term rates.
An open-market sale removes reserves; in the limited-reserves model this tends to raise short-term rates.
Lower administered rates ease monetary conditions; higher administered rates restrain them.
In an ample-reserves system, administered rates are the main tool for controlling short-term rates.
Do not assume every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction. The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.
WORKED EXAMPLE: OPEN-MARKET PURCHASE AND DEPOSIT EXPANSION

The central bank buys $50 million of securities, adding $50 million to bank reserves. With a 20% required reserve ratio, no excess reserves, and full redepositing, the simple deposit multiplier is 1 / 0.20 = 5. Maximum deposit expansion is $50 million x 5 = $250 million. Currency drain or additional reserve holding makes the result smaller; it cannot be calculated by multiplying 5 by the lending share.
If the central bank lowers the rate it charges banks for direct loans, what is the immediate textbook effect?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Limits of Monetary Control
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-22 - Limits of Monetary Control

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate currency drain, excess reserves, leverage risk, and multiplier slippage.

The central bank influences rather than perfectly controls broad money because banks and the public choose how much to lend, hold, deposit, or keep as cash. Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process. If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens. The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits. When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.
The Fed influences the money supply, but banks and depositors affect reserves, lending, and deposits.
When banks hold more excess reserves, they lend less, so deposit creation weakens.
The Fed can influence money creation, but banks and the public also matter.
The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves.
Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks.

Do not treat the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money. The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MONEY EXPANSION FALLS SHORT

The Fed adds $40 million of reserves, but banks hold half as excess reserves and the public keeps some funds as cash. Because only part of the injection supports new loans and redeposits, broad money rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts. The Fed controls reserves more directly than it controls deposits held by the public.
Why is Fed control of the money supply imperfect?
Return to the game and master this concept.
