title: Quantity Theory of Money
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-23 - Quantity Theory of Money

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply the quantity equation, velocity, money growth, price levels, and inflation.

The quantity equation MV = PY links the money stock and velocity to nominal output. Its growth-rate form separates growth in money and velocity from growth in real output and the price level. When velocity is stable and real output is determined by productive capacity, persistent money growth above real-output growth produces long-run inflation rather than permanently higher real output.
The problem uses MV = PY or relates money growth to inflation.
Velocity measures how often money supports transactions during a period.
With velocity and real output fixed, more money raises the price level.
The question distinguishes a nominal price change from a lasting real-output change.
Do not assume money growth permanently raises real output. The quantity theory connects persistent money growth to inflation, especially in the long run.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MONEY GROWTH AND INFLATION

In this clean quantity-theory case, velocity V and real output Y are fixed. Money supply doubles from 2,500 (MS1) to 5,000 (MS2). The value of money falls from 2 at a to 1 at b. Since P is its reciprocal, P rises from 1/2 = 0.50 to 1/1 = 1.00: a 100% increase. The graph shows value of money (1/P), not velocity V in MV = PY.
In MV = PY, what does P represent?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Monetary Neutrality
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-24 - Monetary Neutrality

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish nominal and real variables and analyze long-run neutrality.

Monetary neutrality means that a lasting change in the money supply changes nominal variables but not real output or employment in the long run. Nominal variables changed, but real output did not. Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run. Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.
Separate nominal variables, measured in money, from real variables, measured in goods, services, or purchasing power.
A lasting money-supply change can alter the price level and other nominal values in the long run.
Under monetary neutrality, long-run real output and employment remain determined by real resources and technology.
Do not apply long-run neutrality to the short run, when sticky prices can make money affect real activity.
Do not assume money changes real variables permanently in the long run. Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables in the long run, not real output or employment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NOMINAL VERSUS REAL EFFECTS

With velocity V and long-run real output Y fixed, money supply doubles from 2,500 to 5,000. The value of money falls from 2 at a to 1 at b, so P rises from 1/2 = 0.50 to 1/1 = 1.00: a 100% increase. Prices double while long-run real output does not rise. This is monetary neutrality. Value of money (1/P) is not velocity V in MV = PY.
A student says, “If money is neutral, monetary policy can never affect real output.” What is the best correction?

title: Fisher Effect
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-25 - Fisher Effect

blocks.text: Outcome: Connect expected inflation to nominal and real interest rates.

The Fisher effect links the nominal interest rate to the real interest rate and expected inflation. The nominal rate approximately equals the real rate plus expected inflation, so lenders generally require a higher nominal rate when they expect faster price growth. This adjustment helps preserve the expected real return, though unexpected inflation can still redistribute purchasing power.
The Fisher equation links nominal rates, real rates, and expected inflation: nominal rate approximately equals real rate plus expected inflation.
Nominal interest rates include expected inflation, so they rise when expected inflation rises.
The Fisher effect says higher expected inflation tends to raise nominal interest rates.
Higher expected inflation tends to be built into higher nominal interest rates.
A bank sets a fixed nominal loan rate today for next year.

Do not use realized inflation to explain a nominal rate chosen before the loan was made. The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.
WORKED EXAMPLE: APPLYING THE FISHER EQUATION

Real interest is 2% and expected inflation is 6%. The usual approximation gives nominal interest of 2% + 6% = 8%. The exact compounding calculation is (1.02 x 1.06 - 1) x 100 = 8.12%. At a given real rate, higher expected inflation raises the nominal rate lenders require.
A borrower says the Fisher effect is found by subtracting this year’s actual inflation from a loan rate set last year. What is the key mistake?

title: Costs of Inflation
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-26 - Costs of Inflation

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze redistribution, shoeleather costs, menu costs, and price distortions.

Inflation redistributes purchasing power when it differs from expectations and creates shoeleather, menu, and relative-price costs. Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars. Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices. Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high. Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.
Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and effort people spend reducing money holdings when inflation is high.
Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.
Menu costs are the costs firms face when they change posted prices.
Firms repeatedly changing posted prices incur menu costs.
Menu costs are the costs of changing posted prices.
Do not confuse shoeleather costs with menu costs. Shoeleather costs are the wasted effort people spend trying to hold less money during inflation.

A lender makes a 9% loan expecting 3% inflation, so the expected real return is 6%. Actual inflation turns out to be 10%, making the realized real return approximately 9% - 10% = -1%. Unexpected inflation transfers purchasing power from the lender to the borrower.
A student says, “If everyone correctly expects 6 percent inflation, inflation has no economic costs.” Which response is best?

title: Inflation Tax and Deflation
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-27 - Inflation Tax and Deflation

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze seigniorage, the inflation tax, disinflation, and deflation burdens.

Money creation can finance government spending; the revenue from creating money is seigniorage. When prices rise, existing money balances lose purchasing power, creating an inflation tax on money holders. Disinflation means slower inflation; deflation means a falling price level. Deflation raises the purchasing power of cash but also raises the real burden of a fixed nominal debt.
Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing cash balances.
A fall from 6% to 2% inflation is disinflation: prices still rise.
Negative inflation means deflation: the price level falls.
With a fixed nominal debt, lower prices raise the amount of goods needed to repay it.
Do not assume a tax must always be explicit and legislative. Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.
WORKED EXAMPLE: PURCHASING POWER OF CASH

A household holds $1,000 in cash while the price level rises 10%. Its purchasing power becomes $1,000 / 1.10 = $909.09 in initial-price dollars, a 9.09% loss. If the price level instead falls 10%, a fixed $1,000 debt has a real repayment burden of $1,000 / 0.90 = $1,111.11 in initial-price dollars.
A student looks for an “inflation tax” line on a tax return. What is the best correction?

content.core: Money creation can finance government spending; the revenue from creating money is seigniorage. When prices rise, existing money balances lose purchasing power, creating an inflation tax on money holders. Disinflation means slower inflation; deflation means a falling price level. Deflation raises the purchasing power of cash but also raises the real burden of a fixed nominal debt.

A fall from 6% to 2% inflation is disinflation: prices still rise.
Negative inflation means deflation: the price level falls.
With a fixed nominal debt, lower prices raise the amount of goods needed to repay it.

title: Liquidity Preference and the Money Market
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-28 - Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

blocks.text: Outcome: Determine money-market equilibrium and interest-rate adjustment.
Liquidity Preference and the Money Market

Money-market equilibrium occurs where the quantity of money supplied equals the quantity demanded at a particular interest rate. With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes the interest rate up. Higher money demand with fixed money supply raises interest rates. Liquidity preference theory explains the interest rate as the price that balances money supply and money demand.
Treat the money supply as fixed by policy in the basic liquidity-preference model.
Money demand slopes downward because a higher interest rate raises the opportunity cost of holding money.
The equilibrium interest rate occurs where quantity of money demanded equals quantity supplied.
A money-supply increase lowers the equilibrium interest rate; stronger money demand raises it.

Do not treat a labeled point on a money-supply line as an equilibrium even when it is not on the active money-demand curve. At an interest rate above equilibrium, money supplied exceeds money demanded and asset-market adjustment pushes the rate down; below equilibrium, excess money demand pushes it up.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE MONEY-MARKET RATE

Money supply increases from 100 to 125 while the money-demand curve is unchanged. The added 25 units move equilibrium down the demand curve, lowering the nominal interest rate from 4% to 2%. The graph therefore illustrates how an expansionary money-supply change reduces the short-term interest rate.
At the current interest rate, households want to hold more money than the fixed money supply provides. Which adjustment moves the market toward equilibrium?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Monetary-Policy Transmission
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-29 - Monetary-Policy Transmission

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace monetary policy through interest rates, investment, aggregate demand, and output.

Monetary policy affects output by changing reserves and short-term interest rates, which influence investment, interest-sensitive consumption, and aggregate demand. Expansionary policy increases reserves and tends to lower interest rates, encouraging spending and shifting aggregate demand right. Contractionary policy works in the opposite direction. The strength of the transmission depends on bank lending, borrower response, and spending sensitivity to interest rates.
Begin with the central bank's change in reserves or the money supply.
Trace the resulting change in short-term interest rates.
Connect interest rates to interest-sensitive spending, especially investment and durable consumption.
The spending change shifts aggregate demand and affects output and the price level in the short run.

The graph identifies the direction of the monetary-policy effect, not its size. A multiplier calculation also needs an initial spending change and assumptions about induced consumption and other offsets.

In the money-market panel, contraction from MS1 to MS2 raises the interest rate from r1 to r2. Higher borrowing costs reduce interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts from AD1 to AD2. At price level P1, real output demanded falls from Y1 to Y2. The panels display the complete monetary-policy transmission chain.
A student writes only “the central bank increases money supply, so aggregate demand rises.” Which missing links are essential to the standard short-run transmission mechanism?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-30 - Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace government purchases and taxes into aggregate demand.

Fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through changes in government purchases, taxes, and their effects on consumption. Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left. After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect. A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.
Higher government purchases directly raise aggregate demand; lower purchases reduce it.
Tax changes affect aggregate demand indirectly by changing disposable income and consumption.
Expansionary fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand right; contractionary policy shifts it left.
Distinguish a shift of aggregate demand from a movement along the curve caused by the price level.

A common mistake is to classify fiscal policy from the economy's condition rather than the government's action. Higher purchases or lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases or higher taxes are contractionary.

At the displayed price level P, an expansionary fiscal action shifts aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2. Real output demanded rises from Y1 to Y2 at that fixed price level. A larger action could shift demand to AD3 and quantity demanded to Y3, but the graph does not establish which package is desirable; that depends on the output gap and timing.
Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Fiscal Multipliers and Crowding Out
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-31 - Fiscal Multipliers and Crowding Out

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate multiplier effects and evaluate crowding out.

A spending or tax change can create a multiplied demand response, while higher interest rates can crowd out part of the expansion. Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back. Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise. Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates. In the simple fixed-price model with lump-sum taxes and no import leakage, the spending multiplier is 1 / (1 - MPC), and the tax multiplier is -MPC / (1 - MPC).
Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.
Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.
Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.
A common mistake is to report a gross multiplier effect without subtracting private spending displaced by higher interest rates. Crowding out makes the net demand increase smaller.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MULTIPLIER VERSUS CROWDING OUT

With MPC = 0.8, the simple spending multiplier is 5. A $20 billion increase in purchases raises demand by $100 billion before offsets. In the graph, AD1 to AD3 is the gross expansion; crowding out leaves AD2. At fixed P, real output demanded rises to Y2 rather than Y3. Actual equilibrium output also depends on aggregate supply.
Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Stabilization Policy
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-32 - Stabilization Policy

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate active policy, lags, coordination, automatic stabilizers, and shock response.

Stabilization policy uses fiscal or monetary tools and automatic stabilizers to reduce output gaps and inflation pressure. Expansionary policy supports aggregate demand when output is below potential, while contractionary policy restrains demand when the economy is overheating. Recognition, decision, implementation, and impact lags can weaken or even reverse the intended effect if conditions change before policy takes hold.
Identify whether output is below or above potential and whether inflation pressure is weak or strong.
Expansionary policy supports demand in a recession; contractionary policy restrains excessive demand and inflation.
Automatic stabilizers respond without new legislation, while discretionary policy requires a deliberate decision.
Consider recognition, decision, implementation, and impact lags before judging likely stabilization effects.

Do not treat a negative supply shock as if policymakers can simultaneously eliminate its inflation and output effects by shifting AD. Demand stabilization during a negative supply shock involves a tradeoff: supporting output can worsen price pressure, while reducing inflation can deepen the output loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHEN POLICY ARRIVES LATE

A $30 billion spending increase is enacted during a recession but takes effect after recovery. With MPC = 0.8, the simple multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5, so the planned AD increase is $30 billion x 5 = $150 billion. Arriving after the recession, the stimulus can worsen an overheating gap rather than stabilize output.
Which policy acts automatically to cushion a recession without a new vote by Congress?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Aggregate Demand
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-33 - Aggregate Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain the slope and shifters of aggregate demand.

Aggregate demand shows the total quantity of domestically produced goods and services demanded at each price level. It slopes downward because a lower price level increases the purchasing power of money balances, tends to reduce interest rates, and makes domestic goods relatively cheaper abroad. Consumption, investment, government purchases, or net exports can change for reasons other than the price level; those changes shift the entire aggregate-demand curve.
At each price level, a rightward AD shift means more real GDP demanded.
In the displayed graph, AD1 lies left of AD0, showing a decrease in aggregate demand.
A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper to foreign buyers.
A rise in the price level reduces consumption because money holdings buy less.
Do not confuse the three reasons aggregate demand slopes downward. A lower domestic price level can lower interest rates and the currency value, raising net exports.
WORKED EXAMPLE: A LEFTWARD SHIFT OF AGGREGATE DEMAND

A fall in planned consumption shifts aggregate demand left from AD0 to AD1. At a price level of 60, real GDP demanded falls from about 120 to about 70, a decrease of about 50 units. Spending changes at every price level, so this is a shift to a new AD curve, not movement along AD0.
What change from AD0 to AD1 is shown?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply

blocks.text: Explain the SRAS slope and distinguish movements
Short-run aggregate supply shows the real GDP firms produce at each price level while some wages, input prices, and expectations adjust
slowly. It slopes upward because an unexpected rise in the price level can temporarily raise production profitability. A price-level change
moves along SRAS; changes in input costs, expected prices, productivity, or business taxes shift the entire curve.
A higher current price level, with determinants fixed, means movement up along SRAS.
Higher expected prices or higher input costs shift SRAS left/up.
Lower input costs or higher productivity shift SRAS right/down.
Short-run output can lie above or below potential output because adjustment is incomplete.
Do not shift SRAS merely because the current price level changes. Ask whether production conditions changed at every price level.

title: Short-Run Phillips Curve
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-37 - Short-Run Phillips Curve

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment when expected inflation is fixed. With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC. The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run. The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.
A short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment.
Higher AD raises output and prices, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation.
The short-run Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
A move up and left along the displayed SRPC means lower unemployment and higher inflation.

Do not confuse the Phillips curve with the AD-AS model. The short-run Phillips curve shows that lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment is associated with lower inflation.

title: Long-Run Phillips Curve
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-38 - Long-Run Phillips Curve

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply the natural-rate hypothesis and vertical long-run Phillips curve.

The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural unemployment rate because expected inflation eventually adjusts. A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Expected inflation rises from 2 percent to 5 percent while unemployment remains at its natural rate.
The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.
A national job-matching system reduces the time workers spend searching for suitable positions.

Do not treat a higher expected inflation rate as a permanent way to lower unemployment. Along the long-run Phillips curve, different inflation rates can coexist with the same natural rate of unemployment.
WORKED EXAMPLE: RETURNING TO THE NATURAL RATE

The vertical LRPC is drawn at 5% unemployment. A temporary demand expansion can move unemployment below 5% along a short-run Phillips curve, but expected inflation eventually adjusts and the short-run curve shifts. Unemployment returns to the 5% natural rate at a higher inflation rate, so no permanent tradeoff remains.
Why does higher inflation not permanently lower unemployment in the natural-rate model?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Phillips-Curve Expectations
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-39 - Phillips-Curve Expectations

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze expected inflation and supply shocks as Phillips-curve shifters.

Expected inflation and supply shocks shift the short-run Phillips curve rather than moving the economy along one curve. Higher expected inflation raises actual inflation at each unemployment rate and shifts the curve upward; lower expectations shift it downward. Adverse supply shocks can also raise inflation at a given unemployment rate. A demand change, by contrast, moves the economy along the current short-run curve while expectations remain fixed.
A movement along one short-run Phillips curve reflects a change in aggregate demand with expected inflation fixed.
Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run Phillips curve upward; lower expected inflation shifts it downward.
An adverse supply shock can shift the curve upward by raising inflation at each unemployment rate.
Compare inflation at the same unemployment rate to identify a shift rather than a movement along the curve.
Do not confuse a curve shift with movement along one curve. At the same unemployment rate, a higher SRPC reflects higher expected inflation or a worse tradeoff.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING THE PHILLIPS CURVE

The economy begins at point b on SRPC2 with unemployment U2 and inflation I2. When expected inflation falls, the short-run Phillips curve shifts downward to SRPC1. At the natural unemployment rate U2, the economy reaches point c with lower inflation I1. Expectations, not a permanent unemployment change, drive the shift.

title: Disinflation and Policy
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-40 - Disinflation and Policy

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace monetary disinflation, unemployment costs, and expectations adjustment.

Disinflation lowers the inflation rate but usually creates temporary output and employment costs while expectations adjust. Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
Disinflation means the inflation rate is falling, not that the price level is falling.
Contractionary policy initially moves the economy along the existing short-run Phillips curve toward higher unemployment.
As expected inflation falls, the short-run Phillips curve shifts downward.
Credible policy and flexible expectations can reduce the output and employment cost of lowering inflation.
Do not confuse a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level. Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

Contractionary policy first moves the economy along SRPC2 from b to d, lowering inflation from I2 to I1 while unemployment rises from U2 to U3. As expected inflation adjusts downward, SRPC shifts to SRPC1 and unemployment returns to U2 at point c. Disinflation creates a temporary employment cost.
Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Sacrifice Ratio
documentTitle: Macroeconomics MACRO-41 - Sacrifice Ratio

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output lost for each percentage-point reduction in inflation. Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment. The preferred path depends on credibility, expectations, adjustment speed, uncertainty, and cumulative costs. The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced. If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.
The sacrifice ratio measures how much output is lost when inflation is reduced.
If expected inflation falls faster, the short-run cost of disinflation can be smaller.
The sacrifice ratio measures cumulative output loss per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
A disinflation has a lower sacrifice ratio than another.
Faster adjustment of expected inflation reduces the output cost of disinflation.

A common mistake is to divide the dollar output loss directly by the inflation change. First express the loss as a percentage of potential output, then divide by the percentage-point reduction in inflation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING THE SACRIFICE RATIO

Potential output is $400 billion and cumulative output loss during disinflation is $24 billion. The loss is $24 / $400 = 6% of potential output. Inflation falls by 3 percentage points, so the sacrifice ratio is 6 / 3 = 2: the economy loses 2% of one year's output per percentage-point reduction in inflation.
Should annual output gaps be added before calculating a multi-year sacrifice ratio?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities
documentTitle: MACRO-42 - Saving, Investment, and National-Saving Identities

blocks.text: Calculate private, public, and national saving in
With net taxes T, private saving is Y - T - C and public saving is T - G. National saving is their sum: S = Y - C - G. In a closed economy, S
= I. In an open economy, S = I + NCO; because NX = NCO in the course model, S = I + NX. These are aggregate identities, not claims
that each saver directly funds one investor.
Budget surplus means T - G is positive; a deficit makes public saving negative.
Adding private and public saving cancels T and gives Y - C - G.
Use S = I only for the closed-economy model.
In an open economy, saving can finance domestic investment or net capital outflow.
Do not reverse the public-saving sign. T - G is public saving; G - T is the budget deficit. Also state the closed-economy assumption
WORKED EXAMPLE: FROM COMPONENTS TO OPEN-ECONOMY SAVING
Open: S = I + NCO; NX = NCO
Let Y = $1,200, T = $150, C = $760, and G = $260. Private saving is $290;
public saving is -$110; national saving is $180. If domestic investment is
$140, then NCO = S - I = $40. The accounting identity also gives NX = $40.
Private saving is $220 and public saving is -$50. What is national saving?

title: Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
documentTitle: MACRO-48 - Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data

blocks.text: Interpret debt levels, debt-to-GDP ratios, and
Debt Measures, Debt Burden, and Fiscal Data
The debt level is a nominal dollar stock; the debt-to-GDP ratio compares that stock with the economy's annual income and productive
capacity. Ratios support comparisons across time and economies, but they do not by themselves prove sustainability. Interest rates,

title: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
documentTitle: MACRO-49 - Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier

blocks.text: Deposit Creation and the Money Multiplier
In the simple textbook model, banks keep the required fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. When loan proceeds are
redeposited, another bank can lend part again. The repeated process creates deposits. The simple money multiplier m = 1 / rr gives the
theoretical maximum total deposit expansion per dollar of new reserves under full lending and redepositing.
Required reserves = reserve ratio x deposits; excess reserves can support new lending.
A lower reserve ratio produces a larger simple multiplier.
Each lending round is smaller because a fraction is retained as reserves.
Currency holding and excess reserves make actual expansion smaller than the maximum.
Do not confuse the multiplier with bank capital or claim that one bank lends the entire multiplied amount. The multiplier summarizes
repeated system-wide rounds under restrictive assumptions.
Maximum deposits = new reserves x m
With rr = 10%, the simple multiplier is 1 / 0.10 = 10. If $1,000 of new
reserves enters the banking system, maximum total deposits are $10,000.
Banks collectively retain $1,000 as required reserves and can support up to
$9,000 of new loans. Cash holding or excess reserves lowers the result.
If rr rises from 10% to 20%, what happens to the simple multiplier?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: International Transactions and Open-Economy Identities

blocks.text: Calculate trade and capital balances and connect
Net exports are exports minus imports: NX = X - M. Positive NX is a trade surplus; negative NX is a trade deficit. Net capital outflow is
domestic purchases of foreign assets minus foreign purchases of domestic assets. In the course accounting model, NX = NCO. National
saving finances domestic investment and NCO, so S = I + NCO = I + NX.
Exports add to NX; imports subtract from NX.
A domestic resident buying a foreign asset raises capital outflow and NCO.
A foreign resident buying a domestic asset lowers NCO and is a capital inflow.
If S exceeds I, the difference is positive NCO and positive NX.
Do not import Micro tariff or comparative-advantage analysis into these identities. Also do not call a trade deficit a mathematical error: it
corresponds to negative NCO in the accounting model.

$240 billion, saving is I + NCO = $180 billion.

Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
The nominal exchange rate states how much one currency trades for another. This course uses foreign currency per U.S. dollar for its
dollar-market graphs. A higher value means one dollar buys more foreign currency, so the dollar appreciates; a lower value means dollar
depreciation. Always write the units before converting or interpreting a percentage change.
Foreign currency per dollar: multiply dollars by the quoted rate to obtain foreign currency.
To convert foreign currency back to dollars, divide by foreign currency per dollar.
A rise from 0.90 to 0.99 foreign units per dollar is a 10% dollar appreciation.
The reciprocal quotation moves in the opposite direction.
Never say only 'the exchange rate rose.' Name the quotation. A rise in foreign currency per dollar is dollar appreciation, but a rise in
dollars per foreign currency means dollar depreciation.

title: Price Signals
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-01 - Price Signals

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain how prices coordinate buyers, sellers, and resource allocation.

Prices coordinate decentralized decisions by communicating scarcity and changing the incentives facing buyers and sellers. Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal. A higher price raises the cost of consuming the good and encourages substitution or conservation. A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses. A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.
A higher price communicates stronger scarcity or demand pressure and encourages supply responses.
The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads.
A congested road has no toll.
A price rises while quantity sold also rises.
A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising.

A common mistake is to assume that a higher price always tells buyers and sellers to do the same thing. It discourages quantity demanded while encouraging quantity supplied, coordinating opposite responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: USING A PRICE SIGNAL

A hospital posts current wait times of 90 minutes at Clinic A and 20 minutes at Clinic B. Patients who can use either location shift toward Clinic B. The posted wait acts like a nonmoney price signal: it communicates relative congestion and reallocates demand without changing the medical fee.
What response does a higher market price normally encourage from sellers?

title: Tax Wedges and Revenue
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-02 - Tax Wedges and Revenue

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
Do not use pre tax quantity or buyer price change only. The tax is $46 - $34 = $12. Tax revenue is $12 × 420 = $5,040.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?

title: Market Failures
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-03 - Market Failures

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify externalities, public goods, market power, and corrective policy logic.

A market failure occurs when private decisions do not produce an efficient allocation of resources. An externality affects people outside the transaction. Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.

Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability.
A storm-warning signal can serve another listener without reducing its value and nonpayers are hard to exclude.
Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable; common resources are rival and hard to exclude.
A seller can profitably influence price by restricting output.

Do not confuse government provision with the economic definition of a public good. Public goods are characterized by nonrivalry and nonexcludability. Identify the wedge between private incentives and social value or cost.

A factory's production imposes $8 of pollution damage per unit on nearby residents, but the factory pays only its $20 private marginal cost. Social marginal cost is $20 + $8 = $28. If buyers' marginal benefit is $24, the unit looks worthwhile privately but destroys $4 of social surplus, demonstrating an external-cost market failure.
What makes an effect an externality?

title: Price Elasticity of Demand
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-04 - Price Elasticity of Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand and interpret the result

Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change: PED = absolute percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. The midpoint method uses the average of the two quantities and the average of the two prices, so reversing the direction gives the same result. Demand is elastic when PED is greater than 1, unit elastic at 1, and inelastic below 1. Elasticity uses percentages, not raw unit changes or visual slope. Close substitutes, a longer adjustment period, a larger budget share, and a narrower market definition generally make demand more elastic.
Two price-quantity points are provided for a midpoint calculation.
The problem asks whether the quantity response is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.
Substitutes, time to adjust, budget share, or market scope are changing.
A linear demand curve has constant slope but different elasticity along the line.
A horizontal or vertical demand curve represents a limiting elasticity case.

A steeper-looking curve is not automatically less elastic. Slope uses the original price and quantity units, while elasticity compares percentage changes and depends on the price-quantity location. Put percentage quantity change in the numerator, use midpoint averages in both denominators, and classify demand using the absolute value of PED.

Between C and B, price falls from $12 to $8 while quantity demanded rises from 30 to 60. Using midpoint values, quantity changes by 66.7% and price changes by 40.0%, so PED = 66.7% / 40.0% = 1.67. Because 1.67 is greater than 1, demand is elastic over this interval: quantity responds proportionally more than price changes.
Using points B (P = $8, Q = 60) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), what is midpoint PED, and how should demand be classified over that interval?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Price Elasticity of Supply
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-05 - Price Elasticity of Supply

blocks.text: Outcome: Measure Price Elasticity of Supply.

Price elasticity of supply measures the percentage response of quantity supplied to a one-percent change in price. Price Elasticity of Supply measures and interprets how quantity supplied responds to price changes, including time horizon, capacity, storage, determinants, and midpoint calculations. Storage creates another margin through which sellers can respond to price changes. Investment and capacity adjustment make long-run supply more responsive. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
Look for a percentage change in quantity supplied caused by a percentage change in the good's price.
Compute elasticity as percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
A larger elasticity means sellers respond more strongly to the price change.
Supply is usually more elastic when firms have more time or spare capacity to adjust production.
Do not confuse supply elasticity with demand shifters. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN VERSUS LONG-RUN SUPPLY

The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Income Elasticity of Demand
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-06 - Income Elasticity of Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Income Elasticity of Demand.

Income elasticity of demand measures how demand changes when consumer income changes. Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes. Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes. Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income. A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises.
A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.
Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls.
A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6.
Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.
A common mistake is to misread the sign of income elasticity. A positive coefficient identifies a normal good; a negative coefficient identifies an inferior good.

Household income rises by 10%, and demand for restaurant meals rises by 15%. Income elasticity is 15% / 10% = 1.5. The positive sign identifies restaurant meals as a normal good, and the coefficient above 1 indicates that demand responds more than proportionally to income in this example.
Income changes by 5 percent and demand for premium gym memberships changes by 8 percent. What is income elasticity of demand?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-07 - Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Cross-Price Elasticity of Demand.

Cross-price elasticity measures how demand for one good responds to a price change in another good. A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship. Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good's demand. Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity. Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises.
Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.
Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7.
A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.
The price of Product Y falls 8 percent.
Do not confuse cross price with income or own price. A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.

The price of printers rises by 10%, and demand for ink cartridges falls by 7%. Cross-price elasticity is -7% / 10% = -0.7. The negative sign indicates that printers and ink cartridges are complements because a higher price for printers reduces demand for ink.
The price of Product Y rises 10 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is −0.5. Demand for X is predicted to:?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Elasticity and Total Revenue
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-08 - Elasticity and Total Revenue

blocks.text: Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
For luxury cruise cabins, price changes from $3200 to $2880 while quantity demanded changes from 1,500 to 1,900. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Applications of Elasticity
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-09 - Applications of Elasticity

blocks.text: Elasticity helps predict tax incidence, deadweight loss, pricing responses, and other outcomes that depend on how strongly quantity responds. Market power is stronger when buyers have fewer substitutes. Labor demand is a derived factor demand. The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden. With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.
With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.
More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.
A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1.
Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.
A common mistake is to fail to connect output and input demand. When customers readily reduce output purchases, firms more strongly reduce input use after cost increases.

Two sides of a market face a $6 tax. Buyers have few substitutes and reduce purchases only slightly, while sellers can redirect output to other markets. Demand is less elastic than supply, so buyers bear more of the tax through a larger increase in the price they pay.
If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:?

title: Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-10 - Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay.

Consumer surplus is the difference between a buyer's willingness to pay and the price actually paid. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Demand can be interpreted as buyers' marginal willingness to pay. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
Look for a buyer's willingness to pay and the market price actually paid.
Individual consumer surplus equals willingness to pay minus price.
On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below demand and above the market price up to the quantity traded.
A buyer whose willingness to pay is below price does not purchase and earns no consumer surplus.
Do not assume every trade creates surplus. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.

At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The demand intercept of $30 represents the highest willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is the triangle above price and below demand: 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64.
Why is the rectangle below market price not consumer surplus?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-11 - Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept

blocks.text: Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
Do not confuse wta price gap. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-12 - Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
A common mistake is to fail to separate transfer from total loss. Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Efficient Quantity & Allocation
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-13 - Efficient Quantity & Allocation

blocks.text: The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
A common mistake is to equate more output with more efficiency. The forced extra unit contributes $23 - $29 = -$6 to total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE EFFICIENT QUANTITY

Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.

title: Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-14 - Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace Changes in Surplus & Policy Effects.

A price or policy change can transfer surplus between buyers and sellers and can destroy surplus by preventing mutually beneficial trades. A transfer changes who receives existing gains without changing their total. Deadweight loss is different: it represents gains from exchange that disappear because quantity moves away from the efficient level.
Establish the initial consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus before the change.
Recalculate those areas after the price change or policy intervention.
Separate transfers between buyers and sellers from surplus that disappears entirely.
Deadweight loss represents mutually beneficial trades prevented by the change.

A common mistake is to count only existing buyers or only new buyers. With the same trades still occurring, the price change transfers surplus dollar for dollar from sellers to buyers; it does not change total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRANSFER OR DEADWEIGHT LOSS?

At price P1 = $12, quantity is 8 and consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($20 - $12) = $32. At P2 = $8, quantity rises to 12 and consumer surplus becomes 1/2 x 12 x ($20 - $8) = $72. The price decrease raises consumer surplus by $40.
A policy transfers $20 to consumers and prevents $6 of gains. Total-surplus loss?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-15 - Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis.
Efficiency, Equity & Limits of Surplus Analysis

Efficiency concerns the size of total surplus, while equity concerns how benefits and costs are distributed. The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.
Use total surplus to evaluate efficiency and distributional evidence to evaluate equity.
Recognize that the allocation with the largest total surplus need not be the most equal.
Remember that measured willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay.
A policy judgment requires an explicit value choice when efficiency and equity point in different directions.

Do not treat efficiency as equity. Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power. A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WEIGHING EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY

Policy A creates $500 of total surplus divided evenly between buyers and sellers. Policy B creates $520 of total surplus but gives $500 to sellers and $20 to buyers. Policy B is more efficient because total surplus is larger, but whether its distribution is more equitable is a separate normative judgment.
A student says efficiency requires equal gains. Correction?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-16 - Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities

blocks.text: Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
A common mistake is to omit one or more welfare components. Revenue is tariff×imports; each side distortion is a triangle. Total DWL is $144.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
Using the import-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and imports at Pw=$30?

title: Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-17 - Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers.

International trade changes consumer and producer surplus and creates net gains when the world price differs from the no-trade equilibrium price. The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.
Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.

Do not assume trade has only winners or only losers. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers. The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING TRADE WINNERS AND LOSERS

At the $30 world price, domestic producers supply 10 units and domestic consumers demand 50, so imports equal 40. Relative to the $50 no-trade equilibrium, the two gain-from-trade triangles each have base 20 and height 20. Their combined area is $200 + $200 = $400.
Why do consumers gain when a lower world price opens an import market?

title: Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-18 - Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost.
Economic Costs: Explicit, Implicit & Opportunity Cost

Economic cost includes both explicit payments and the implicit opportunity costs of owner-supplied resources. Explicit costs require cash payments to outside suppliers, while implicit costs measure the value of income or returns forgone by using the owner's time, money, or property in the business. Economic decisions count both because every resource has a next-best use.
Classify cash payments to outside suppliers as explicit costs.
Identify the income or return sacrificed on owner-supplied time, money, or property as an implicit cost.
Economic cost includes both explicit and implicit opportunity costs.
Do not treat an owner-supplied resource as free merely because no check is written.
A common mistake is to count only recorded expense. Economic cost equals explicit cost plus all implicit opportunity costs: $70,000 + $40,000 + $5,000.

A business pays $70,000 in wages and rent. The owner also gives up a $40,000 salary and $5,000 of interest that invested capital could have earned elsewhere. Explicit cost is $70,000; implicit cost is $45,000; economic cost is $70,000 + $45,000 = $115,000.
Which cost belongs in economic cost but not recorded accounting cost?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Accounting, Economic & Normal Profit
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-19 - Accounting, Economic & Normal Profit

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate and interpret accounting profit, economic profit, implicit costs, and normal profit.

Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs from revenue, while economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs. Normal profit is the return required to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use, so it is included among implicit costs. Zero economic profit therefore means the firm covers every explicit and implicit cost, not that the owner receives nothing.
Start with total revenue and identify both explicit and implicit costs.
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs only; economic profit subtracts both kinds of cost.
Normal profit is the owner's opportunity cost and is included among implicit costs.
Zero economic profit can coexist with positive accounting profit.

Do not treat zero economic profit as failure. Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources. The $85,000 accounting profit exactly covers the $85,000 of implicit opportunity costs.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ACCOUNTING VERSUS ECONOMIC PROFIT

A firm earns $200,000 of revenue and pays $115,000 of explicit costs, so accounting profit is $85,000. If the owner's forgone salary, interest, and rent also total $85,000, economic profit is $85,000 - $85,000 = $0. The firm still earns normal profit because its resources receive their opportunity-cost return.
A firm earns zero economic profit. What has it covered?

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Production & Diminishing Marginal Product.

In the short run, at least one input is fixed, so output changes as additional units of a variable input are employed. Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost. The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

title: Cost Components & Cost Schedules
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-21 - Cost Components & Cost Schedules

blocks.text: Outcome: Complete short-run cost schedules using total and average cost identities

In the short run, total fixed cost (TFC) does not change with output, while total variable cost (TVC) rises or falls as production changes. Total cost combines both components: TC = TFC + TVC. For positive output Q, divide each total by Q: AFC = TFC / Q, AVC = TVC / Q, and ATC = TC / Q = AFC + AVC. At zero output, TVC is normally zero, TC equals TFC, and average costs are undefined because division by zero is impossible. On a total-cost graph, the vertical distance between TC and TVC equals TFC at every quantity.
A cost-schedule row is missing TFC, TVC, or TC.
A fixed payment remains even when current output is zero.
A cost changes when labor, materials, or production changes.
The vertical gap between TC and TVC is compared across quantities.
Total costs must be converted to per-unit AFC, AVC, or ATC.

Do not subtract or multiply fixed and variable cost when finding total cost: add them. Also distinguish total fixed cost from average fixed cost. TFC stays constant as output changes, but AFC = TFC / Q falls as the same fixed amount is spread across more units. Average costs are not defined at Q = 0.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BUILDING A COST SCHEDULE

At Q = 120, the graph shows total cost of $1,200 and total variable cost of $800. The $400 vertical gap between the two curves is total fixed cost because TC = TFC + TVC. Dividing each cost by 120 gives AFC = $3.33, AVC = $6.67, and ATC = $10.00. As a check, AFC + AVC = ATC.
At Q = 10, a schedule shows TFC = $90 and TC = $250. What are TVC, AFC, AVC, and ATC, and how can you verify that AFC + AVC = ATC?

title: Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-22 - Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
A common mistake is to misuse average cost formula. AVC = $300/20 = $15; AFC = $5; ATC = $20. TVC = $1,000; AVC = $20, AFC = $8, and ATC = $28.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.

title: Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-23 - Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages.

Marginal cost is the change in total cost caused by producing one more unit. Divide the input cost by marginal product. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
Look for the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit.
Compute marginal cost as the change in total cost divided by the change in output.
A fixed-cost change does not change marginal cost, but a variable-input cost change usually does.
When marginal product falls, marginal cost tends to rise if the input price is unchanged.
A common mistake is to move mp and mc together. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LINKING MARGINAL PRODUCT AND COST

Marginal cost crosses AVC at AVC's minimum of $10 and 200 units, then crosses AC at AC's minimum of $20 and 400 units. When marginal cost is below an average, it pulls that average down; when marginal cost rises above it, the average begins to increase.
If output rises by 1 unit and total cost rises by $18, marginal cost of that unit is:?

title: Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-24 - Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Cost Curves: Relationships & Shifts.

Short-run cost curves move differently because fixed costs affect AFC and ATC, while variable-input costs affect AVC, ATC, and MC. A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down. Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
A technology improvement reduces the variable input needed at every output.
Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.
A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output.
A common mistake is to mix fixed and variable shifts. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING SHORT-RUN COST CURVES

Suppose the firm signs a more expensive lease while output and variable input prices are unchanged. The higher fixed cost raises average fixed cost and therefore shifts ATC upward. AVC and MC remain in the positions shown because neither depends on fixed cost. The production decision at the margin is unchanged.
Why does the ATC–AVC gap shrink?

title: Sunk & Avoidable Costs
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-25 - Sunk & Avoidable Costs

blocks.text: Sunk costs cannot be recovered and should not affect a current decision; avoidable costs change with the option chosen. Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision. The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment. The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options. Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.
Ask whether a cost has already been incurred and cannot be recovered.
Exclude sunk costs from the comparison among current options.
Include avoidable costs because they differ depending on which option is chosen.
Focus on future benefits and future costs that change with the decision.
Do not treat fixed as sunk. The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options. Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IGNORE OR INCLUDE THE COST?

A theater has already paid a nonrefundable $4,000 license fee. Canceling tonight's show avoids $3,000 of staffing and utility costs but gives up $5,500 of ticket revenue. The sunk $4,000 does not affect the current decision. Because operating adds $5,500 - $3,000 = $2,500, the theater should hold the show.
A fixed annual license can be surrendered halfway through the year for a $4,000 refund. For a midyear shutdown decision, which amount is relevant?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-26 - LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret LRAC, Economies & Diseconomies of Scale.

Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable cost per unit when every input and plant size can vary. Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary. Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.
Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale.
The concepts apply to different horizons and input changes.
A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate.
Do not confuse scale and diminishing returns. Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING LONG-RUN AVERAGE COST

The LRAC curve falls from about $20 at 30 units to its minimum of about $12 at 60 units, showing economies of scale. It then rises back toward $20 by 90 units, showing diseconomies of scale. The cost-minimizing scale is approximately 60 units.
The graph gives roughly the same LRAC at Q=30 and Q=90. Which statement distinguishes those two positions?

title: Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-27 - Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale.
Minimum Efficient Scale & Constant Returns to Scale

Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which long-run average cost reaches its minimum. Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached. MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.
Find the lowest point of the long-run average-cost curve.
Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which that minimum cost is attained.
A flat minimum indicates a range of outputs with constant returns to scale.
Do not confuse a flat average-cost segment with output remaining unchanged.
A common mistake is to invent flat lrac region. The graph has a single rounded minimum rather than a visibly flat minimum-cost interval.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MINIMUM EFFICIENT SCALE

The LRAC curve reaches its lowest value, about $12 per unit, at an output of 60. Minimum efficient scale is the smallest output that attains minimum long-run average cost, so the graph's MES is 60 units. Outputs below 60 have not exhausted economies of scale.
If LRAC first reaches its minimum at 5,000 units and remains flat until 8,000, MES is:?

title: Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-28 - Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue

blocks.text: Outcome: Connect Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue.
Market Structure, Price Taking & Firm Revenue

A perfectly competitive firm takes the market price as given, so price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal. Market power changes the firm's revenue conditions; the competitive firm takes price. Price taking makes each sold unit add the same amount to revenue, setting up the later MR-versus-MC output rule.
Look for many firms, a standardized product, easy entry, and no control over market price.
A price-taking firm can sell another unit without lowering its price.
For the competitive firm, price, average revenue, and marginal revenue are equal.
Treat market price as a horizontal line in the individual firm's graph.
A common mistake is to separate price, average revenue, and marginal revenue for a price-taking firm. Under perfect competition, P = AR = MR.
WORKED EXAMPLE: REVENUE FOR A PRICE TAKER

The competitive firm takes the market price of $25, so P = MR = AR. The horizontal price line meets marginal cost at 50 units, and total revenue is $25 x 50 = $1,250. Because ATC is also $25 at that output, the firm earns zero economic profit.
Why does total revenue rise linearly with output?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-29 - Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule.
Profit-Maximizing Output & the MR = MC Rule

A firm maximizes profit or minimizes loss by producing the quantity where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue. The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR. Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost. Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.
Use the firm's marginal-revenue curve and the rising portion of marginal cost.
Choose the output where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, provided the firm should operate.
If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, another unit raises profit; if marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, it lowers profit.
Do not choose output by minimizing average total cost unless that output also satisfies the marginal rule.
A common mistake is to misapply competitive firm rule. Market price becomes the firm’s MR, linking market equilibrium to the firm’s marginal output choice.
WORKED EXAMPLE: USING THE MR = MC RULE

The firm's market price and marginal revenue are $25. The rising marginal-cost curve reaches $25 at 50 units, so the last unit adds exactly as much revenue as cost. Producing fewer units leaves profitable output unmade; producing more makes MC exceed MR. Profit-maximizing output is 50.
MR is $25 and the next unit’s MC is $19. What should the firm do?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Profit, Loss & Break-Even
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-30 - Profit, Loss & Break-Even

blocks.text: Economic profit or loss equals the gap between price and average total cost multiplied by output. Profit, Loss & Break-Even measures per-unit and total economic profit or loss and interpret break-even and zero economic profit. The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit. Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons. Separate output, operating status, profit or loss, and long-run entry or exit pressure.
First find the firm's chosen output using the marginal-revenue and marginal-cost rule.
At that output, compare price with average total cost.
Price above average total cost means profit; equality means break-even; price below average total cost means loss.
Measure profit or loss as the per-unit gap multiplied by output.

Do not confuse loss with shutdown. Profit/loss measurement and the short-run shutdown decision use different comparisons. Economic cost includes implicit opportunity costs, including the normal return needed to keep owner resources in the firm.
WORKED EXAMPLE: PROFIT, LOSS, OR BREAK-EVEN?

The market sets a price of $15. The representative firm produces 50 units where P = MR = MC, but its ATC is $18. Loss per unit is $18 - $15 = $3, so total loss is $3 x 50 = $150. The firm may still operate because price exceeds AVC.
How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-31 - Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply Shutdown & Short-Run Loss Minimization.

A firm should operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost, even if price is below average total cost. A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost. AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run. Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating.
Find the profit-maximizing or loss-minimizing output where marginal revenue equals rising marginal cost.
At that output, compare price with average variable cost.
Operate in the short run when price covers average variable cost; shut down when price falls below it.
A firm may operate at a loss when it covers variable cost and contributes something toward fixed cost.

A common mistake is to misapply competitive firm rule. Short-run loss minimization compares the incremental benefit and avoidable cost of operating. A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHUT DOWN OR OPERATE?

The horizontal price line is $10, below minimum AVC of $20 at point A. At every positive output, revenue per unit would be less than avoidable variable cost. The firm minimizes its short-run loss by shutting down and paying only fixed cost.
P is below minimum AVC. What should the firm do?
