title: Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-32 - Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.

A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.

Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 33 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-33 - Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace entry, exit, zero economic profit, normal profit, and long-run competitive adjustment.

Entry and exit move a competitive industry toward long-run equilibrium with zero economic profit. More firms supply more total output at each price. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.
Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
Long-run industry assessment 10: Demand falls in a constant-cost industry and some firms leave.
Long-run industry assessment 11: Demand rises in a constant-cost industry and entry is unrestricted.

Do not miss long run equilibrium conditions. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY AND ZERO ECONOMIC PROFIT

The market equilibrium price is $25. At that price, the representative firm produces 50 units where P = MC, and $25 is also the minimum ATC. Revenue covers all explicit and implicit costs, so economic profit is zero and no entry or exit pressure remains.
Why can accounting profit be positive at zero economic profit?

title: Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-34 - Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions

blocks.text: Outcome: Distinguish Long-Run Industry Supply & Cost Conditions.

Long-run industry supply depends on how industry expansion changes firms' input costs. The long-run industry response can feed back through shared input markets. The slope depends on how industry expansion affects input costs and firms' cost curves.
In a constant-cost competitive industry, industry expansion leaves input prices and firms’ cost curves essentially unchanged.
A learner interprets a downward-sloping long-run industry supply curve as a violation of competition.
Short-run market adjustment creates the profit signal; entry and cost conditions determine the long-run destination.
Read only the relationships displayed and apply the competitive-firm sequence in the correct order.
Do not confuse industry cost conditions. If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING LONG-RUN INDUSTRY SUPPLY

The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward, rising from roughly $18 at very low output to above $50 near 105 units. Industry expansion therefore raises the long-run equilibrium price. That pattern is consistent with an increasing-cost industry in which entry bids up specialized inputs or other production costs.
Graph analysis 13: What can produce the downward-sloping long-run industry supply shown?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Competitive Efficiency & Model Limits
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-35 - Competitive Efficiency & Model Limits

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret Competitive Efficiency & Model Limits.

Perfect competition is allocatively efficient when price equals marginal cost and productively efficient when firms produce at minimum average total cost. The benchmark requires private and social marginal costs to align. Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions. Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.
Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.
Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.
A representative competitive firm is in long-run equilibrium at the minimum point of ATC.
Price reflects marginal willingness to pay while MC reflects marginal opportunity cost.

A common mistake is to equate efficiency with equity. Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions. Minimum average total cost represents the least-cost scale for producing that output in the benchmark.

At the long-run competitive outcome, the firm produces 50 units where price equals marginal cost and price also equals minimum ATC at $25. P = MC gives allocative efficiency, while production at minimum ATC gives productive efficiency. These conclusions depend on the competitive model's assumptions.
P=MC and P>min ATC. Which interpretation is strongest?

title: Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-36 - Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly.
Monopoly Power, Barriers to Entry & Sources of Monopoly

A monopoly has durable market power because barriers prevent close rivals from entering and eroding that power. Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets. Natural monopoly can make one-firm production cost-efficient while still creating a market-power problem.
A city has one coffee shop today, but entry is easy and several rivals are preparing to open.
A software firm is the only seller this year.
The current one-seller market does not by itself establish durable monopoly power.
One seller becomes a durable monopoly only when entry is meaningfully blocked.

Do not treat any large firm as monopoly. Durable monopoly power depends on the relevant market and barriers to entry. A monopoly requires meaningful barriers to entry, not merely one seller at a moment in time.

Across the relevant output range, the graph's ATC curve declines as output expands, so one large producer can supply the market at lower average cost than several small firms. That cost structure supports natural monopoly. At the efficient point where demand meets MC, price would be below ATC, creating a regulatory funding problem.
Which fact most strongly supports classifying a firm as a monopoly?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-37 - Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue

blocks.text: Outcome: Interpret Monopoly Demand, Revenue & Marginal Revenue.

A monopolist faces the market demand curve, so selling another unit requires a lower price and makes marginal revenue less than price. A price taker sells each unit at the same price; a monopolist lowers price to expand output. Price taking removes the price effect that drives monopoly MR below price.
Start with the monopolist's downward-sloping market demand curve.
Because selling another unit requires a lower price, marginal revenue lies below demand.
For a linear demand curve, marginal revenue shares the vertical intercept and falls twice as quickly.
Marginal revenue is positive where demand is elastic and negative where demand is inelastic.
A common mistake is to equate mr and price. Linear MR shares demand’s vertical intercept and is twice as steep. For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.
WORKED EXAMPLE: WHY MR FALLS BELOW PRICE

At 40 units, the demand curve shows a price of $40, while the marginal-revenue curve shows MR of $20. Total revenue is $40 x 40 = $1,600. The gap between price and marginal revenue illustrates why a monopolist's MR lies below demand when lowering price is necessary to sell another unit.
For a single-price monopolist, which curve gives price at each output?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-38 - Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price

blocks.text: Outcome: Apply Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price.

A monopolist chooses output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue, then uses demand to determine price. Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost. MR is compared with MC for output choice. Find Q from MR=MC, then read price from demand. Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.
Find output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.
Keep the output decision and price decision separate: marginal conditions determine quantity, demand determines price.
Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.

The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.
What is the correct order for solving a monopoly graph?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Monopoly Profit, Loss & Shutdown
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-39 - Monopoly Profit, Loss & Shutdown

blocks.text: Outcome: Calculate Monopoly Profit, Loss & Shutdown.

Monopoly profit or loss is measured after the profit-maximizing output and demand-based price have been found. The firm must cover avoidable variable cost. Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis. Profit or loss equals (P−ATC)Q at the chosen output.
Choose monopoly output where rising marginal cost equals marginal revenue, then read price from demand.
At that output, compare price with average total cost to determine profit or loss.
Compare price with average variable cost to decide whether a loss-making monopolist operates in the short run.
Measure profit or loss as the price-cost gap multiplied by output.

A common mistake is to mix output choice with profit measurement. Output optimization and profit measurement are separate steps in monopoly analysis. Profit or loss equals (P−ATC)Q at the chosen output.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MONOPOLY PROFIT OR LOSS
The firm chooses 36 units where MR equals MC. At that output, demand gives a price of $42 and ATC is $27. Profit per unit is $42 - $27 = $15, so total economic profit is $15 x 36 = $540.
Why does P>MC not prove positive economic profit?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-40 - Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison

blocks.text: Outcome: Compare Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison.

Compared with competition, monopoly usually restricts output, raises price, transfers surplus, and creates deadweight loss. Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not. The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
Compare monopoly output and price with the competitive benchmark where price equals marginal cost.
Monopoly normally produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
Separate the transfer of surplus to the monopolist from surplus lost through reduced output.
Deadweight loss is the value of trades between monopoly output and the efficient quantity that no longer occur.
A common mistake is to reverse monopoly competitive comparison. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MONOPOLY DEADWEIGHT LOSS

The unregulated monopoly chooses about 45 units where MR = MC and charges the demand price of about $47. The efficient outcome occurs where demand meets MC: 90 units at $20. Monopoly therefore restricts output and raises price, leaving mutually beneficial units between 45 and 90 unproduced.
Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?

title: Natural Monopoly & Regulation
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-41 - Natural Monopoly & Regulation

blocks.text: A natural monopoly has declining average cost across the relevant market range, making one large producer less costly than several small firms. The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC. Average-cost pricing is a compromise between cost recovery and the P=MC efficiency benchmark. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC.

Marginal-cost pricing expands output toward efficiency but may leave the firm unable to cover average cost.
Average-cost pricing can preserve financial viability but produces less than the efficient quantity.
Evaluate regulation by comparing price, output, efficiency, and the need for subsidy or allowed profit.

Do not confuse allocative efficiency with break even. Marginal-cost pricing can require financial support when MC lies below ATC. Natural monopoly is rooted in cost structure and economies of scale rather than legal exclusion alone.

Marginal-cost pricing sets demand equal to MC, which the graph shows at 140 units and $10. ATC there is about $15, so the regulated firm would lose about ($15 - $10) x 140 = $700. Average-cost pricing near 115 units and $16 avoids that loss but leaves price above marginal cost.
What is the main compromise under average-cost pricing?

title: Price Discrimination
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-42 - Price Discrimination

blocks.text: Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same product when resale can be prevented. Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist. Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable. Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.

Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.
The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.
Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.
A common mistake is to disconnect wtp from first degree efficiency. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.

A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.
Can ordinary group price discrimination increase total welfare?

title: Market Structure & Product Differentiation
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-43 - Market Structure & Product Differentiation

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify Market Structure & Product Differentiation.

Monopolistic competition combines many firms and relatively easy entry with differentiated products and limited price-setting power. Entry and exit operate in both models. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry. The practice is differentiating the service experience rather than relying on a legal barrier or identical product. Differentiation makes the firm’s product an imperfect substitute, so its individual demand curve slopes downward.
A market has many sellers and easy entry.
A dental practice competes mainly through evening hours, online scheduling, and unusually fast appointments.
A restaurant has many nearby rivals, but customers value its menu and atmosphere enough that a small price increase does not drive everyone away.
A market has many small sellers and easy entry, but every seller offers exactly the same product.
A neighborhood café competes through atmosphere, menu, and location.
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation explains why an individual firm faces downward-sloping demand despite many sellers and easy entry.

A city has many coffee shops, entry is relatively easy, and each shop offers a distinct menu and atmosphere. Because customers view the shops as close but imperfect substitutes, each shop faces downward-sloping demand and has limited price-setting power. Those facts identify monopolistic competition.
Why is a differentiated firm’s demand downward sloping?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-44 - Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown

blocks.text: Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

The firm chooses 36 units where MR = MC at $15, then charges $27 on its demand curve. ATC is also $27, so total revenue and total cost are both $27 x 36 = $972. Economic profit is zero, but P > MC shows the outcome is not allocatively efficient.
A firm has P>MC but P<ATC. Which statement is correct?

title: Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-45 - Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium

blocks.text: Outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

At 36 units, the firm charges $27 and has ATC of $27. Total revenue is $27 x 36 = $972, and total cost is also $972, so economic profit is zero. With no profit attracting entry and no loss causing exit, the industry is in long-run equilibrium.
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-46 - Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition.

Advertising can provide information, persuade buyers, build a brand, and change the elasticity or position of a firm's demand curve. The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price. In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales. A fixed selling cost raises fixed and average total cost but does not directly raise MC or AVC. The ad is trying to shape preferences and brand perception rather than mainly transmit facts.
A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged.
Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase.
A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand.
A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information.
A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive.

A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. The firm is competing through product features and service rather than changing price. In signaling models, willingness to incur a visible selling cost can sometimes convey information when higher quality supports repeat sales.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INFORMATIVE OR PERSUASIVE ADVERTISING?

A pharmacy advertises that a prescription costs $8 and that it stays open until 10 p.m. Buyers can compare stores more easily, so search costs fall; this is informational advertising. A separate campaign associates the brand with status without adding product facts; that campaign is persuasive advertising. Both compete without directly cutting price.

Monopolistic competition trades some cost and allocative efficiency for product variety and differentiated consumer choices. Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain. Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

title: Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-48 - Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration

blocks.text: Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.

An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.

The graph shows market shares of 38%, 32%, 12%, 9%, and 9%. HHI equals the sum of squared shares: 38^2 + 32^2 + 12^2 + 9^2 + 9^2 = 1,444 + 1,024 + 144 + 81 + 81 = 2,774. That value indicates substantial concentration.
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-49 - Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium

blocks.text: Outcome: Read payoff matrices and identify best responses, dominant strategies, and Nash equilibrium.
Game Theory Foundations: Payoff Matrices, Best Responses & Nash Equilibrium

Game theory represents strategic choices with players, actions, and payoffs that depend on what others do. Correctly reading the matrix is the prerequisite for identifying best responses and equilibrium. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
Identify the players, each player's available actions, and the payoff associated with every action combination.
For each possible rival action, mark the action that gives a player the highest payoff.
A dominant strategy is best regardless of the rival's action.
A Nash equilibrium is a cell where every player's action is a best response to the others.
Do not assume equilibrium is efficient. Compare mutual best responses with the combined-payoff maximum. A Nash equilibrium is a cell containing mutual best responses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NASH EQUILIBRIUM

For each strategy of the other player, mark the action that gives a player the larger payoff. In the displayed matrix, row A against column X gives (9, 9), while switching unilaterally to row B would lower the row player's payoff from 9 to 3. The column player also prefers X to Y when row A is chosen, so (A, X) is a cell of mutual best responses and is a Nash equilibrium.
Why must payoff order be stated?

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives.

A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.

The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.

A cartel acts like one monopolist and selects industry output where industry MR equals MC. On the graph, the downward-sloping MR curve meets the $20 MC line at 20 units. The cartel then uses demand to set price. Each member has an incentive to sell extra units, which makes the agreement unstable.

title: Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-51 - Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence

Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence examines repeated interaction, credibility, commitments, limit pricing, entry deterrence, continuation incentives, and sequential strategic reasoning. A higher continuation factor increases the weight on future consequences. Cooperation PV is 12.50; cheating path PV is 16.25. Net gain = 25 − 8 − 14 = 3 million. Aggressive competition and predation must be distinguished with evidence.
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
Do not assume every low price is predatory. Net gain = 25 − 8 − 14 = 3 million. Aggressive competition and predation must be distinguished with evidence.

title: Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-52 - Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition

blocks.text: Outcome: Analyze Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition.
Tacit Coordination, Price Leadership & Nonprice Competition

Tacit coordination occurs when firms align behavior without an explicit agreement, while nonprice competition uses quality, service, or advertising rather than price cuts. Advertising can shape demand in both markets. Strategic interdependence applies to quality, advertising, service, and other competitive dimensions as well as price. Tacit coordination refers to aligned behavior without the explicit agreement that defines collusion.
A student has learned that oligopoly firms react strategically to price changes.
A student says tacit coordination and explicit collusion are identical.
Tacit coordination can arise through expectations and repeated conduct.
A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price.
Do not assume price is irrelevant. Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions. A leader’s announced price can become a focal point.

title: Oligopoly Welfare, Mergers & Antitrust Tradeoffs
documentTitle: Microeconomics MICRO-53 - Oligopoly Welfare, Mergers & Antitrust Tradeoffs

blocks.text: Outcome: Evaluate Oligopoly Welfare, Mergers & Antitrust Tradeoffs.

Oligopoly and merger policy weighs the risk of reduced rivalry against verifiable efficiencies, innovation, entry, and consumer effects. Policy weighs market-power risk against verifiable benefits. A sound evaluation combines structure, strategic conduct, efficiency claims, and market responses. The core welfare concern is reduced rivalry that raises prices, restricts output, and can create deadweight loss. Oligopoly welfare requires integrating several margins rather than treating one statistic as decisive.

A concentrated industry has high prices, strong product innovation, and frequent entry by niche rivals.
A student sees several firms charge the same price and immediately labels the behavior collusion.
A merger creates a larger research budget but also reduces head-to-head price competition.

A common mistake is to equate cartel profit with dwl. DWL is the triangle between demand and MC over the lost output. Oligopoly policy requires evidence about conduct, entry, efficiencies, and consumer effects.

A merger raises the HHI and may increase market power, but the statistic alone is not the verdict. Suppose the merged firm can cut marginal cost by $4 per unit and entry remains easy. An antitrust evaluation compares the likely price and output effects of reduced rivalry with the verifiable efficiency and entry evidence before reaching a conclusion.
Does a higher post-merger HHI settle the welfare question?

blocks.text: Recognize when an equal-sized loss affects choice
Loss aversion means that people often experience a loss as more consequential than an equal-sized gain, measured relative to a
reference point. This asymmetry can make giving something up feel more important than acquiring the same amount.
Identify the reference point that separates a perceived gain from a perceived loss.
Compare reactions to changes of equal magnitude in opposite directions.
Reluctance to give up something already owned can reflect the same asymmetry.
The key evidence is stronger weight on the loss, not simply dislike of uncertainty.
Loss aversion is not identical to risk aversion. Risk aversion concerns uncertainty; loss aversion concerns asymmetric reactions to
losses and equivalent gains around a reference point.
WORKED EXAMPLE: EQUAL DOLLARS, UNEQUAL WEIGHT
A student uses the expected account balance as a reference point. An
unexpected $50 refund produces mild pleasure, while an unexpected $50 fee
produces much greater distress. The dollar changes are equal in magnitude, but
the $50 loss receives greater psychological weight than the $50 gain. That
asymmetry around the reference point is evidence of loss aversion.
Someone is much more upset by losing $20 than pleased by gaining $20. Which comparison supports loss aversion?
Return to the game and master this concept.

title: Framing Effects

blocks.text: different decisions because of their description.
A framing effect occurs when presenting economically equivalent information in different ways changes choice. A gain frame and a
loss frame can draw attention to different features even though the underlying outcomes are the same or nearly the same.
First verify that the underlying outcomes are economically equivalent or nearly equivalent.
Compare gain wording with loss wording, such as survival versus mortality.
Equivalent discounts and surcharges can also create different reactions through framing.
A changed choice caused by presentation, rather than outcomes, is the diagnostic clue.
Framing requires equivalent underlying alternatives. If costs, probabilities, or consequences actually differ, a different choice may be
rational rather than a framing effect.
A treatment is described to one group as having a 90% survival rate and to
another as having a 10% mortality rate. The probabilities describe the same
outcome. If acceptance changes merely because one statement emphasizes
survival and the other emphasizes death, the wording—not an economic
difference—changed choice. That response is a framing effect.

title: Condorcet Paradox & Voting Cycles
documentTitle: MICRO-66 - Condorcet Paradox & Voting Cycles

blocks.text: Explain how pairwise majority rule can generate
Even when every voter has a consistent ranking, pairwise majority voting can produce a cycle: A defeats B, B defeats C, and C
defeats A. The group then has no option that defeats every alternative, and agenda order can affect the final outcome.
There are at least three alternatives and voters rank them differently.
Compare alternatives two at a time using majority rule.
The collective relation cycles even though each individual's ranking is consistent.
Because no option is a universal majority winner, agenda order may matter.
A voting cycle does not require irrational voters. Individually transitive rankings can aggregate into an intransitive majority relation.

Voter 1 ranks A > B > C; Voter 2 ranks B > C > A; Voter 3 ranks C > A > B.
Against B, A wins with Voters 1 and 3. Against C, B wins with Voters 1 and 2.

title: Median Voter Theorem
documentTitle: MICRO-68 - Median Voter Theorem

blocks.text: Explain why majority-rule competition can favor the
median voter's position under specific assumptions.
When policy lies on one dimension, preferences are single-peaked, and decisions use majority rule, the median voter's preferred
position has a special advantage. Policies or candidates may move toward it because alternatives on either side can be defeated by a
Place voters along one policy dimension and identify the middle preferred position.
Each voter has a single peak and prefers positions less as they move away from it.
Competition can favor the median, but the conclusion depends on these assumptions.
The median voter does not always decide elections. Multidimensional policy, non-single-peaked preferences, turnout, institutions, or
other departures can break the result.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THE PIVOTAL POLICY POSITION
Five voters prefer policy levels 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. The ordered middle
preference is 30. Against a proposal below 30, the voters at 30, 40, and 50 form
a majority for 30; against one above 30, the voters at 10, 20, and 30 form a
majority for 30. Under one-dimensional, single-peaked preferences and majority
rule, the median position can defeat alternatives on either side.
